title: Olympic equestrian says whipping ban stems from illegal video recording
text:
Olympian Heath Ryan has added international horse sport officials to a lawsuit he launched over a ban for whipping a horse.

Earlier this year, the Hunter-based horseman lodged a civil suit against Equestrian Australia over what he alleged was its reliance on an "unlawful video recording" in findings made against him.

The organisation imposed an 18-month ban after findings that he had whipped a six-year-old horse called Nico more than 40 times.

His lawyer, Kyle Kutasi, today said his client had been treated unfairly and would be including the sport's global governing body, the Federation Equestre Internationale (FEI), in his suit.

"He has suffered reputational damage and was suspended without proper process," he said.

"The video was taken out of context and Mr Ryan is now unable to compete and some people have stopped bringing horses to him to train or break in."

Heath Ryan says he was acting in the horse's best interests. (ABC News)

The Swiss-based FEI denounced Mr Ryan's conduct after seeing the video. It found he had brought "equestrian sport into disrepute and breached welfare standards".

"Each strike followed the last with no pause and no hesitation, leaving the horse no opportunity to respond," the FEI said in the judgement that led to the ban.

"Even a single whip may be excessive if applied with too much force."

Reputational damage

In August, an FEI tribunal issued the 18-month ban, backdated to July last year, and fined Mr Ryan $5,170.

Under the ban, Mr Ryan cannot take part in any competition or FEI‑related activity, including coaching of FEI athletes.

"The Horse displayed signs of pain, distress and fear," the tribunal said in its judgement.

"It kicked out, backed up, swished its tail and moved its head.

"That reaction, together with the audible sound of the whip, demonstrated that the strikes were excessive and caused the horse significant pain."

Olympian's defence

Mr Ryan, who represented Australia in dressage at the Beijing Olympic Games in 2008, has said the ban and fine stemmed from a video that was filmed illegally and out of context.

At the time the vision emerged online, the equestrian published a statement on his Facebook page.

The tribunal referred to that statement, in which Mr Ryan had said he was acting in the horse's best interests.

Heath Ryan is seeking damages from Australian and international equestrian officials. (ABC News)

Mr Ryan said the horse came to him after an accident that resulted in a female rider needing hospital treatment.

"All I can say is that this awful video was collateral damage of me from the bottom of my heart launching a rescue mission," his Facebook statement said at the time, claiming the horse would otherwise have been sent to a knackery.

When the video first emerged, Mr Ryan, 68, justified his actions in a social media post which described the horse as "uncontrollable".

"I have never ridden anything like [Nico]," he said in the statement.

"I am so sad this was caught on video. If I had been thinking of myself I would have immediately just gotten off and sent Nico to the knackery.

"That video was a life-or-death moment for Nico and of that I was very aware."

Papers served in Switzerland

In a lawsuit first mentioned in the Supreme Court in July, documents were lodged on behalf of Mr Ryan seeking interim injunctions against Equestrian Australia Limited over what he alleged was an unlawful video recording.

The case was back in court for a brief directions hearing today.

Mr Kutasi told the court papers were also being served on the FEI.

Heath Ryan is an Olympian and equestrian coach. (ABC News)

"The second defendant is a foreign-registered corporation, and service is required to be done in accordance with the Hague Convention," Mr Kutasi said.

The Hague Service Convention is an international agreement that makes it easier to serve a legal document from one country to another in civil or commercial cases.

Mr Kutasi said he was advised two weeks ago that service on FEI had "now been undertaken".

The case has been adjourned to December 10.

title: Brewers complete underdog story with maiden World Series title
text:
The small-ball Milwaukee Brewers, playing in the smallest market in the majors, are World Series champions for the first time.

Young ace Jacob Misiorowski threw 5 2/3 scoreless innings, rookie Cooper Pratt had two more hits and two runs batted in (RBIs), and the Brewers beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 to set off a long-awaited celebration among thousands of Brewers fans in attendance at Tropicana Field.

"It's the best feeling ever. All of our fans are here. I know the city's waited a long, long time for this," Milwaukee captain Christian Yelich said.

"We're so happy to bring it home to them. I can't wait to get back there and celebrate."

World Series MVP William Contreras hit an RBI double and Misiorowski allowed just two hits before leaving the game because of a right calf cramp. He got a standing ovation from the Brew-Crew fans, who took over the section behind Milwaukee's dugout for the last three games.

The 22-year-old Pratt set a series rookie record with six straight hits before a sacrifice fly in the sixth. Jackson Chourio set a five-game series record with 11 hits.

"This is one of the greatest moments of my life. Oh my gosh. It doesn't even feel real," said Pratt, who made his major league debut in June.

"This is surreal. It only took four months."

The championship comes in the 58th season for a franchise that began as the Seattle Pilots in 1969 and moved to Milwaukee the following year. The Brewers' only previous trip to the World Series in 1982 ended in heartbreak when they blew a 3-1 lead in the sixth inning of Game 7 and lost 6-3 to the St. Louis Cardinals.

But this team displayed the toughness and resilience of 67-year-old manager Pat Murphy, who survived a heart attack in 2020 and was the NL Manager of the Year in his first two full seasons at the helm in 2024 and 2025.

"This group of guys right here, the 2026 team, will be remembered forever — and they deserve that because they were a team," Murphy said.

"When you talk about this team, you've got to talk about people who care about each other. They're not worried about their own stats. No-one cares about that. They care about coming together and winning tonight."

AP

title: Highly invasive weed threatening native flora and fauna at Uluru
text:
Uluru is arguably the nation's most recognised and revered landmark, but concerned tourism operators and rangers say the World Heritage site is facing a growing crisis.

Highly invasive buffel grass, which is known to choke native plants, destroy animal habitats and elevate fire risk, is blanketing the base of the sacred site and its neighbouring Kata Tjuta rock formations.

According to a handout from Parks Australia, which manages the Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park, buffel grass was introduced in the late 70s "around the base of Uluru to reduce erosion from four-wheel drive vehicles".

"It now thrives in this area," it reads.

The NT government declared buffel grass a weed in 2024. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

Parks Australia says the weed has now infested about 2,650 hectares of the national park, equating to 2 per cent of its total area.

Tracey Guest has worked in and around the park for more than two decades, including as a Parks Australia manager, helping protect the natural and cultural values of the area before her recent retirement.

During that time, she was on the front line of the fight against the aggressive weed, including co-authoring papers and sitting on an NT government advisory committee about buffel.

Tracey Guest says buffel grass covers about 90 per cent of the land at the base of Uluru. (Supplied)

Ms Guest said buffel grass was "concentrated around the rock and Kata Tjuta", covering "maybe 90 per cent around the base of Uluru, except for where we've done some management".

"Buffel grass is the biggest threat to the World Heritage values, the cultural, natural values, of Uluru," she said.

"It's a very clever grass that has done a job way better than it was first anticipated and it's now become an environmental weed equal to the cane toad in Australia."

Native plants cannot compete

Ms Guest said this year had been one for the wildflower, a time when the local Aboriginal Anangu people say "country's really strong".

"But when you have the buffel grass covering all that, no one gets that sensation of the country and lifting your spirits and being exciting," she said.

"This year should be the year of the pretty flower; it should be amazing, yet we've got buffel grass where those sort of plants would grow.

Buffel grass is visible all around the base of Uluru. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

"Nothing will come up around it because it just sends this toxin into the soil that's protecting itself from competition.

" It's just covering country and nothing else is able to compete against it. "

On the outskirts of the park, the Tjakura rangers work to care for the Katiti Petermann Indigenous Protected Area (IPA).

Part of their work is managing buffel grass alongside other park rangers, neighbouring Indigenous ranger groups and pastoralists, to prevent it from choking vital habitat.

Garth Forrester, an Anangu traditional owner, is the regional coordinator overseeing the IPA under the Central Land Council.

Mr Forrester said when buffel grass spreads, "it's indiscriminate, it takes over things".

Garth Forrester says the community is concerned about the spread of buffel grass. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

"Looking around where we're standing now, you're just seeing spinifex, and you're seeing all the beautiful wildflowers and vegetation," he said.

"But if we drive away from here, just about 10 or 20 minutes down the road, you'll see where the buffel grass is starting to come in and impact.

"Our constituents are that worried about the buffel grass that we have acquired funding to get two brand new spray units to be able to combat the oncoming buffel grass."

Calls for action to avoid 'significant negative impacts'

Tourism Central Australia chief executive Danial Rochford said operators across the region were seeing the effect of buffel grass on the landscape, especially after recent weather created ideal conditions for the fast-growing weed to flourish.

"Most of our visitors aren't aware of buffel grass," he said.

Danial Rochford says there needs to be more resources made available to address buffel grass at Uluru. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

"But what our members are seeing is its impact to the flora and fauna.

"This is a weed that is permeating through very sensitive parts of Central Australia.

"We will have significant negative impacts if we don't deal with buffel grass in the short term."

Mr Rochford said urgent investment was needed to tackle the problem head-on.

"We need to see resources flow through to manage this on the ground, otherwise we're just not going to be able to put the cat back in the bag," he said.

Uluru is sacred to the Anangu people of the region. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

"We are not going to be able to eradicate buffel grass in totality; that's never going to happen, but there are places where we can draw a line in the sand.

" Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park is a perfect example of where we should be putting significant resources. "

In a statement, a Parks Australia spokesperson said buffel grass management was "specified as a priority" under its management plan and "a combination of mechanical removal, chemical treatment and drone technology" was used to monitor and manage buffel grass.

Solutions from the past

Ms Guest said a volunteer program and effort by parks staff in the early 2000s had helped to contain the weed.

"The park actually had a good program at that stage," she said.

"The conservation volunteers would come down and spend … the winter months digging out, paying to dig out, buffel grass around the rock.

Tracey Guest says in the 2000s buffel grass was better managed. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

"And there was a lot of work done, and we were actually making headway through that time, and that program stopped in 2010.

"There wasn't enough follow-up."

Ms Guest said follow-up required vigilant, relentless work over extended periods.

"The follow-up is the most important element around managing buffel grass," she said.

"You can go and spray a big area, and if you don't do the follow-up, it'll be back again in 12 months."

The spread of buffel grass is negatively affecting the growth of native flowers, such as yellow billy buttons. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

She said reinstating a volunteer program or welcoming students undertaking a relevant TAFE or university course could also help.

"It is a no-brainer," she said.

"You need people that are bush regenerators, people that are physically able and interested in doing that sort of work and want to make a difference to the place," she said.

Art show highlights buffel grass devastation An art exhibition opening in Alice Springs today will shine a spotlight on the native plants driven out of Central Australia by buffel grass.

"You'd have a double whammy because you have cultural induction.

"So understanding how First Nations people look at the world so you get their view, and working alongside people is better than just having some class where someone talks at you."

She said new technology is also offering some light at the end of the tunnel.

"There's new things coming through that can help us manage buffel grass, and the more interest that we put on this, the more effort people will put into finding solutions," she said.

"If we do nothing, it's actually going to cost us way more. So we have to do something."

title: Club's social media post 'deeply troubling' after coach charged with rape
text:
The Northern Tasmanian Football Association says it is "deeply troubled" by a country football club's social media activity, after its former coach was charged with three counts of rape.

Former Bracknell Football Club coach Josh Adams is facing rape charges, with police confirming they charged a 44-year-old man with the offences, alleged to have occurred in April last year.

He is scheduled to appear in the Launceston Magistrates Court early next year.

An independent media outlet first reported the charges, and also detailed private messages exchanged between Bracknell Football Club president Nicole Jones and the mother of Mr Adams's alleged victim.

Ms Jones then apologised and resigned.

But the ABC has since seen copies of a post on the club's Facebook page calling for the club to stand together and saying "we must remember that people are more than headlines, allegations or one difficult chapter".

"We cannot let division tear apart something that has brought so many people together," the post also said.

" And we cannot allow this chapter to become the final chapter of something so special. "

AFL Tasmania said it was now reviewing related social media activity for potential breaches of the National Community Football Policy Handbook.

It said it would work with the Northern Tasmanian Football Association (NTFA) and the club to ensure these matters were appropriately addressed.

The NTFA said it was "deeply troubled" by the recent events involving Bracknell Football Club and subsequent social media activity.

It said it recognised the distress these circumstances may have caused, particularly to the alleged victim and others affected.

"The club has been asked to cease public commentary about this matter that may cause further distress or harm to those involved," it said.

'Safeguarding responsibilities' to be highlighted

The NTFA said it would engage directly with its member clubs to reinforce their safeguarding responsibilities, expected standards of conduct and obligations when responding to allegations of sexual violence and other serious misconduct.

Tasmanian football club coach charged with rape A former Tasmania football club coach has been charged with three counts of rape, and the club's president has resigned.

It also said it would engage "an appropriately qualified practitioner to provide practical guidance and education to clubs and their volunteers, particularly in responding to disclosures and allegations of sexual violence in a trauma-informed, respectful and accountable manner".

It said it had a pre-existing safeguarding framework, to which all clubs were required to commit.

"Community football should be an environment where everyone feels safe, supported and respected," it said.

"The NTFA is committed to maintaining those standards, strengthening safeguarding practices across its competition and holding its member clubs accountable to the expectations they have committed to uphold."

Association says it 'acted promptly'

The NTFA said it became aware Mr Adams was expected to face serious criminal charges on October 16.

It said it became aware of concerning messages attributed to Ms Jones days later on October 23.

It said it "acted promptly" referring the matter to the AFL for independent consideration and making clear its expectation that the president stand aside from all official club duties.

The president subsequently issued an apology and stood down.

"The NTFA also made clear that the former president was not to continue exercising any official responsibilities within the club while stood down," the NTFA said.

Neither the NTFA or AFL Tasmania said when they first became aware of the allegations about Mr Adams, but have said the circumstances surrounding the criminal allegations remain before the courts and a matter for the police.

The Bracknell Football Club has been contacted for comment.

title: Aussie captain most expensive player at WPL auction
text:
Australia captain Sophie Molineux has proved the most expensive buy in India's Women's Premier League auction, and she'll suit up for a UP Warriorz side captained by former national team skipper Meg Lanning.

With many of the world's top players having already been retained for the 2027 edition of the lucrative Indian league, Molineux's signature was the most coveted one still left and the Lucknow-based franchise captured the T20 World Cup-winning skipper for the biggest price, INR 1.1 crore ($A164,000).

The spinning all-rounder won't be leading the team in the January 14-February 7 tournament, though.

Instead, Molineux will be playing under the captaincy of 34-year-old Lanning, the inspirational figure who skippered Australia when she first came into the side, in a T20I in India eight years ago.

Big life changes for WBBL winning duo A lot has changed since Nicola Carey and Elyse Villani lifted the WBBL trophy last year, as the Hobart Hurricanes prepare to defend their title.

Molineux's base price in the auction in Kochi was 50 Lakh ($A75,000) but she eventually went for over twice that price as a bidding battle began between Royal Challengers Bengaluru and the Warriorz.

With their superior budget, UP also snapped up big-hitting all-rounder Grace Harris going for $45,000, meaning that the side will have four Australians in their ranks with Phoebe Litchfield already on board.

Intriguingly, national skipper Molineux has been bought for less than both Lanning and Litchfield and four others among the 14-strong Australian contingent in the league.

The most expensive Australian in the league — each of the five teams has at least one Aussie World Cup winner in its ranks — will be Ash Gardner, captain of the Gujarat Giants, who was retained for $523,000 in a side that also includes four Aussies.

Gardner is the joint most-lucrative retention, alongside Royal Challengers Bengaluru captain Smriti Mandhana and Mumbai Indians' England skipper Nat Sciver-Brunt.

Of the 11 Australians up for grabs in Wednesday's auction, only three were sold.

Heather Graham, Tayla Vlaeminck, Tess Flintoff, Charli Knott, Samantha Bates, Maitlan Brown, Maddie Penna and Milly Illingworth were the ones to miss out.

title: Gold Coast Suns AFLW finals feat faces home-ground headache
text:
The Gold Coast Suns have earned their place in the AFLW finals — but their reward could be a home final away from home.

After back-to-back seasons near the bottom of the ladder, the Suns have surged into fourth spot with eight wins, booking their first finals appearance since 2023.

A victory over GWS on Sunday would strengthen their grip on a double chance, guaranteeing a home final during the series.

But there's a catch.

Carrara Stadium is unavailable for weeks two, three and four of the finals series, due to Australia's T20 clash with England, leaving the Suns and the AFL searching for an alternative venue.

Springfield, home of Queensland rivals the Brisbane Lions and an hour's drive up the highway, and Southport's Fankhauser Reserve are among the alternatives being considered.

Southport however comes with a significant caveat — any final would need to be played during the day, when November temperatures average around 28 degrees and humidity can hover around 70 per cent.

A spokesperson for the club said it is "working with all stakeholders on home venues for each week of the finals" where Carrara is not available.

"Our playing group and staff have been resolute all season in their efforts to play anywhere, anytime, across eight different venues and we know they'll take that attitude into any scenario that presents throughout the post-season campaign," the spokesperson said.

Despite this, coach Rhyce Shaw said on Tuesday the club is embracing the excitement of a long-awaited finals campaign.

Michael Voss Oval in Springfield is being considered as one option for an alternative venue. (Supplied: Brisbane Lions)

"I took [my son] Henry to swimming the other day and all the staff were getting behind us," Shaw said.

"It is exciting for our footy club … It's been a bit of a tough year all round, but for our girls to pick up the slack a little bit and get going and make finals is really, really cool."

"We've got a big job against the Giants and then we'll think of finals after that."

If the Suns were to fall to GWS on Sunday, there is the potential for them finish as low as seventh on the ladder.

However, a fifth or sixth place finish would mean they would earn a home final next weekend and the ABC can confirm Carrara Stadium would be available in this instance.

Rhyce Shaw, Senior Coach of the Suns, says it's been a "tough year" for the club. (Getty Images: Maya Thompson)

ABC Sport AFLW expert Chyloe Kurdas said regardless of the ladder outcome, the lack of venue certainty is an unwanted distraction.

"I think it is such a valuable home ground advantage [finishing in the top four] but it's also not just that, it's the distraction of this conversation right now that happens in the lead up to," she said.

"It occupies bandwidth and it occupies energy from the playing group and the coaching group and the staff."

Kurdas said not being able to play at Carrara, a venue the side has won their last three games at, would be a missed opportunity.

"I think there's a real sweet spot right now with the number of talented kids that are Gold Coast born and raised … that are now playing at the Suns," Kurdas said.

"Fan engagement is going to be such an important part of this Gold Coast Suns women's team journey … they're so talented."

The Suns have had a 75 per cent increase in AFLW memberships for this season.

A familiar problem

The Suns aren't the only club caught in a scheduling squeeze.

Second-placed Geelong, one win away from securing a top-two finish, also faces a venue clash, with Kardinia Park unavailable next weekend due to the AUSX Supercross Championship.

While, the AFLW Grand Final, should it be played in Melbourne, has already been locked in for Princes Park — with a capacity of 13 thousand that has sold out for the showpiece game within hours in recent seasons.

Docklands Stadium, with a 53,343-capacity is unavailable, with Harry Styles booked across the weekend, despite players calling for a bigger venue.

The Geelong Cats are facing a similar venue problem. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The Grand Final has also been scheduled for Friday night, November 27, to avoid a clash with the Victorian State Election.

It's a familiar problem that's haunted the competition since it started in 2017.

In the inaugural season, the Brisbane Lions earned the right to host the Grand Final but were forced to play at Carrara, with the Gabba unavailable due to cricket.

Now in its 11th season, the debate continues about where the AFLW competition belongs in the sporting calendar.

The AFL is reportedly considering an earlier start to align the women's season with the end of the men's competition.

"You do your due diligence and you look at where is there likely to be these kind of clashes," Chyloe Kurdas said.

"But ultimately, whenever you choose to play it, you then have to live and die by those decisions."

She says clubs and the AFL must also be prepared to make commercial decisions that put their women's programs first.

" You can't just buy in when it suits you. "

The AFL and Stadiums Queensland were contacted for comment.

title: Readers share why and how they are avoiding AI
text:
Have you embraced or rejected AI?

We recently asked three AI experts if the idea that "if you don't use AI, you'll be left behind" was true, and found there is a difference between not using, and ignoring, the technology.

Keen to hear more, we invited readers who are avoiding AI to write in and share why.

L Lia, 18, Sydney/Gadigal Country As a university student, generative AI is all around me and is used by students and staff alike. I refuse to engage in any use of generative AI, or optional AI. I use browser extensions to block Google's AI summary. I turn off AI in any program I use. I do not engage with programs like ChatGPT and Claude. And I actively avoid and block any social media content that uses AI. Society is obsessed with accelerationism without [defining] what exactly we are rushing towards. I fear that AI is not the answer to our problems and will only make the solutions even more difficult to reach.

S Samantha, 55, Northam WA/Ballardong Noongar country AI terrifies me. We had enough trouble knowing what was real, what was true before this, what hope have we got now?

T Tayla, 43, Victoria I work for a company that went from "Do not use AI under any circumstances" to "Use AI for everything" in the blink of an eye. I am greatly concerned about the environmental impacts of AI and have decided to be a conscientious objector on that issue alone. I have openly declared my refusal to go out of my way to use AI at work (yes, I know it can't be completely avoided) and have been told by local IT that "I will be left behind". I am also concerned that people will gradually lose the ability to think for themselves on a broad scale. How many of us remember multiple phone numbers anymore? Imagine that on a broad scale, frightening. Sadly, I know there won't be any satisfaction in being able to say, "I told you so."

R Rainer, 64, Sydney/Gadigal Country I've been a professional driver for 42 years. I developed an ability to read a street map, way before AI or Google came on the scene. I would imprint this map into my brain and then drive the route as outlaid and with accordance to my experience. Surprisingly, there were times when I used Google Maps for a bit of fun and indeed, it showed me a better way. Here's the thing; I used it once to get to an unfamiliar place, then did the drive again without its help and promptly took the wrong exit. This shows exactly [what I think is] the biggest error in learning via AI: you don't learn, you simply follow instructions.

title: Australia records highest rates of anorexia and bulimia globally
text:
Cases of anorexia and bulimia nervosa are affecting Australians at a world-leading rate.

The unenviable record comes amid a 71 per cent increase in cases of the two eating disorders globally in the past 30 years.

This jump translates to about 18.1 million people worldwide living with anorexia or bulimia as of 2023, according to a study published today in JAMA Psychiatry.

Australia has the highest rate of any country in the world, with 1,026.5 per 100,000 people estimated to have one of the two disorders.

University of Queensland epidemiologist and study senior author Damian Santomauro said Australia's ranking was "surprising and concerning".

"Usually we do see higher prevalence of eating disorders in high-income settings," he said.

"[But] I'm surprised to see it as high as it actually is compared to the US or other locations in Western Europe."

Eating disorders disproportionately affect younger people and are a mental health condition involving an unhealthy relationship with food.

Butterfly Helpline clinical psychologist Sarah Cox said the study confirmed what people with lived experience of eating disorders, their families and healthcare professionals had been reporting for years.

"Eating disorders are serious mental illnesses that affect a significant number of people in Australia, and that the number of people affected is growing," Ms Cox said.

How data was calculated

The findings are part of the Global Burden of Disease study, the world's largest health project that includes research about the impact of mental disorders on the overall population.

Global mental health disorder cases double in three decades A surge over the last three decades means mental disorders now account for more than 17 per cent of all disability worldwide, according to a report published this week.

"It was the first of its kind that really highlighted that mental disorders can be on par or if not more burdensome than some physical disorders," Dr Santomauro said.

To calculate the prevalence of these disorders, researchers use surveys rather than treatment data to ensure they capture people who may not have access to treatment.

This allows them to analyse data from around the world since 1990, when the study began.

Worldwide, the researchers estimated 3.92 million people had anorexia and 14.2 million had bulimia. They forecasted cases would keep growing through to 2050 globally.

They also calculated that for the two eating disorders, that led to a loss of 3.81 million disability adjusted life years around the world.

Dr Santomauro noted that Australia's high number of cases may be partially due to the way survey data was collected.

"Almost all the surveys that are done in Australia tend to use a different methodology [to the rest of the world]," he said.

"But I don't think that it's purely because of that type of data."

Ms Cox said the numbers, while high, might also mean Australia had more research and data.

"We might be seeing the problem more clearly than other countries," she said.

Impact higher for youth and females

Dr Santomauro was not surprised cases had increased globally, and said that although there were many factors, one "hypothesis" was increased time online.

"I would expect prevalence to get worse in more recent years because of social media, the Instagram and body image issues that youth are encountering today," he said.

Females accounted for nearly 70 per cent of the 18.1 million global cases and about 41 per cent of all global cases were in young people aged 10 to 24.

Jeanette Chan, an economist and public policy professional who has lived experience with an eating disorder, said people from migrant and non-western backgrounds could have more difficulty gaining help for eating disorders.

"Growing up as a migrant, I didn't have a lot of language or understanding around what mental health was or what mental health issues were," they said.

"In Australia, we're a very multicultural society, and eating disorders are often a very Western conceptualisation of issues surrounding food and eating.

"That affects the way that we make sense of what is problematic."

Jeanette Chan says community was extremely important for her recovery from an eating disorder. (Supplied: Jeanette Chan)

While Jeanette was able to gain help for her eating disorder, they said more funding for treatment and prevention was needed.

"There's been a lot more investment, but not enough in eating disorders in Australia over the last several years," they said.

Case numbers are underestimated in Australia and abroad

While Australia had the highest rates, the largest relative increases in the incidence of anorexia and bulimia occurred in East Asia, South Asia, and South-East Asia.

The study noted a few limitations, including data gaps for mortality related to bulimia, as well as less information from some low-income countries.

Dr Santomauro said the impact of eating disorders broadly was also underestimated since only anorexia and bulimia were included.

"The numbers … sound very, very large, but it's also really capturing a small proportion of the total eating disorder burden globally.

"There's also binge eating disorder, unspecified feeding or eating disorder and other very prevalent eating disorders that we don't capture."

Ms Cox agreed.

"In Australia, more than 1.1 million people will experience an eating disorder in any given year," she said.

"While anorexia and bulimia are serious eating disorders worthy of attention, we also need to expand the research focus to ensure people living with … other eating disorders are included in the conversation. "

Ms Cox said projections that cases would continue to rise highlighted the need to fund early treatment and prevention.

"We can lower these numbers, and there is more that can be done," she said.

"Getting help early improves the chances of recovery, but many people face barriers to care, including cost, living in regional areas and stigma, and many people with an eating disorder never get treatment."

title: WBBL winning duo on eve of big life changes
text:
A lot has changed since Nicola Carey hit the winning runs for the Hobart Hurricanes in last year's WBBL final.

Cricket-wise, her partner Elyse Villani retired and handed over the captaincy.

Life-wise, they're building a house together and are expecting their first child.

"Now that you've pointed it out, I am a bit overwhelmed," Carey joked.

"We've got a bit going on, don't we?

"Poor thing, Elyse has to carry the baby and do all the admin for the house. We're both very much looking forward to having a little one.

"People keep asking me if I'm excited, but I don't think I know fully what's coming."

The desire to start a family influenced Villani's decision to call time on her WBBL career.

The 37-year-old played in every season since the competition started in 2015 and skippered three different clubs during that time.

Elyse Villani retired last year, and Nicola Carey has since taken over the Hurricanes' captaincy. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

"Elyse would've played cricket forever, but I don't think her body would've allowed it," Carey said.

"It definitely did play a part, but it's not a guaranteed thing that you'll fall pregnant either."

Following successful IVF treatment, Villani is due to give birth to a boy in November.

Loading Instagram content

It was a fairly straightforward process, and Carey said she was grateful knowing how tricky fertility could be for some people.

They are adjusting to the new chapter in their lives, as the Hobart Hurricanes open their season against the Melbourne Stars tonight.

Name game

In February, all-rounder Carey played her first match for Australia in four years.

There has been a lot of interstate travel since and overseas tours to the Caribbean and the UK.

Nicola Carey played in Australia's recent T20I series against New Zealand in Sydney. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

"Elyse came over to England for about seven weeks because I was there for the T20 World Cup and The Hundred, and she was calling it a baby moon," Carey laughed.

"She knows a lot of the players obviously, so it was a huge social get-together and cruisy for her.

"While I was stressed playing terrible cricket she was living her best life."

"No-one misses pre-season do they. Maybe when we start playing again here for Tassie, she'll miss it a bit more."

The couple is aligned when it comes to baby names.

"We've got a few names picked out but we haven't nailed one down yet," Carey said.

"Every male that we walk past seems to have an opinion though.

"Our CEO [at Cricket Tasmania] Dominic Baker is like, 'Dom's a good name,' and I'm thinking, that's not even top 100 for us, but thank you for your input."

Reflecting on the final

The Hurricanes' victory last December at Bellerive Oval was a dream come true: playing in front of their home fans, claiming a maiden title and sending off Villani in style.

The Hurricanes celebrate last year's WBBL title. (Getty Images: Steve Ball)

Although Carey was the batter that sealed the result with a boundary, she concedes she had "the easy part" thanks to a record-breaking innings from teammate Lizelle Lee.

The South African opener was the star of the night, as the team chased down 138 runs.

Blasting 77 off 34 balls, Lee equalled the highest individual score in a WBBL finals match.

The women were inspired after watching their male counterparts lift the BBL trophy in January that same year.

It also followed the achievements of a core group of players in the 50-over Women's National Cricket League (WNCL), clinching three consecutive titles from 2022 to 2024.

The result capped off a wonderful career for Villani, who had previously played in three losing WBBL finals.

The Hurricanes' WBBL title win last season was a special occasion for the players. (ABC News)

She caught the team by surprise, deciding to retire on the spot and go out on a high.

"I sort of knew it was Elyse's last season," Carey said.

"What I didn't know was that she was going to announce it right then and there.

"She was panicking because she told the TV broadcast in an interview first and was then like, 'Oh no, now I need to tell the girls.'

Loading Instagram content

"That caught me off guard.

"To finally win one in your last season adds to that fairytale narrative.

"We had a great group and really good people, which made it enjoyable, so to cap it off with that win was really special."

Despite originally hailing from NSW and Victoria, the couple has now been living in the Apple Isle for a long time and is passionate about ensuring the next generation of the state's talent is set up for sustainable success.

"It's been a nice period of cricket in Tasmania," Carey said.

"A lot of us aren't from there originally, but they've taken us in and welcomed us.

"Because it's so small, everyone lives five minutes away, so you spend a lot more time together than you would in the bigger cities, where you're more spread out.

"It's got a real family feel, so it's nice to be able to give back."

title: ATSB confirms plane landed on Lake Eyre after pilot became unwell
text:
Details are emerging regarding the rescue of two people who landed a plane in Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre after the pilot became unwell.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau has confirmed a plane landed in the lake last week, sustaining minor damage when its propeller struck the ground.

Two people were rescued from the Sling 4 light plane. No injuries were reported.

The two people in the plane were taken to Marree uninjured. (Supplied)

An Australian Maritime Safety Authority spokesperson said it had tasked Santos's Moomba-based helicopter to assist in the rescue on October 19, after contacting the pilot.

The authority said it was alerted to the incident by local flight operator Wrightsair.

Landing aircraft on the lake is prohibited without emergency necessity under the National Parks and Wildlife Act 1972, as is swimming, boating and driving.

The plane was airlifted out of the lake a few days after the incident. (Supplied: Mike Kellow)

The Civil Aviation Safety Authority, which is in charge of ensuring compliance with aviation regulations, said it was aware of the incident, but could not comment on individual cases due to privacy obligations.

Access to the lake on foot has been prohibited since early 2025.

Lake has crusty layer on top of bog

In 1964, Sir Donald Campbell broke the land-speed record when he reached an average of 649 kilometres per hour atop a dry Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre.

Marree-based pilot Tekin Benli said this feat made some people overly confident in the land's strength.

Loading...

"Some people believe, because his four-and-a-half tonne car could do about 650km/h, their little 1-tonne plane can land on it no worries," he said.

"But after a bit of rain, like we had rain a few days before that guy landed, it would have left a bit of a bog underneath and a thin crusty layer of salt over the top.

"So it may look dry in some areas, but you go to land and you'll break through the crust and get into the bog below."

Tekin Benli was flying on the morning of the incident, but did not see it take place. (Supplied: Tekin Benli)

While it is not legally required, Mr Benli said the usual practice for flying over the lake involved communicating movements via a designated radio frequency.

"It's very much recommended ... general aviation pilots pretty much police their own separation," he said.

Record-breaking rain and flooding has filled the lake to its highest level in decades this year.

title: They called him ‘Temu Postecoglou’. Now this Aussie coach has Beckham and Co in his corner
text:
Advertisement

SportSoccerEngland They called him ‘Temu Postecoglou’. Now this Aussie coach has Beckham and Co in his corner Vince Rugari October 29, 2026 — 3:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Peter Cklamovski has spent more time than anyone else riding shotgun with Ange Postecoglou - so for him, a rocky start to a new job is not just familiar terrain, but preferred. This time around, the rocks were extra jagged. Loading Being a self-proclaimed Postecoglou “disciple” was an advantage not so long ago. Now, post-Tottenham, and post-Nottingham, Postecoglou’s reputation in England has taken a battering, as unfair as that may be, to the point where even those who have worked with him are tainted by association. So when Cklamovski lost his first three matches in charge of English fourth-division club Salford City this season, some online critics swiftly settled on a nickname for him: ‘Temu Postecoglou’. Or ‘Temu Ange’, or any such derivative. The inference is clear, and it stings: he is a lesser version of a coach they don’t rate.

Advertisement

Cklamovski can only chuckle. “That’s modern-day football, modern-day society,” he tells this masthead. Peter Cklamovski and his long-time mentor, Ange Postecoglou, after a match between Shimizu S-Pulse and Yokohama F. Marinos. Getty “I’m proud of my connection with Ange, and I want to be a proud extension of his legacy. That’s how much I love the guy. Within that, there’s no secrets. They know, they’ve learned that I’m an Ange disciple, let’s say - so I guess there is a bit of a stigma to that, potentially. “But that’s all noise. If I do my job, and do it well, and do it the way I know I can, then that will be the way we can build something that we dream about. Stay humble, take the bullets when needed, no problem - but don’t let it knock you down.”

Advertisement

Such is the fickle nature of the game that those same supporters who wanted him gone a couple of months ago are probably now singing his name. Salford City are cruising on top of the table amid a club-record seven-game winning streak, and Cklamovski has just been named League Two’s manager of the month. It’s still early days - there are still 33 more games to be played this season - but they are hot favourites to be promoted, and some of the sport’s biggest names are swooning about the aggressive and relentless attacking football Cklamovski has them playing. Jorge Grant celebrates a goal for Salford City against Walsall. Getty Images Indeed, this is no ordinary club. Of all the teams in England’s Football League - the umbrella organisation for the three tiers below the Premier League - Salford City is arguably the best-placed to trace a similar arc as Wrexham and rise up the pyramid, powered by celebrity investment.

Advertisement

Actually, they kind of invented the concept of ‘doing a Wrexham’. In 2014, five members of Manchester United’s fabled Class of ’92 - Gary Neville, Phil Neville, Paul Scholes, Ryan Giggs and Nicky Butt - purchased the club, which is only a short drive from Old Trafford, and only a kilometre from where they used to train together. David Beckham later joined the ownership group, and their early efforts to lift the then-little-known club from the obscurity of England’s eighth division were captured in a fly-on-the-wall documentary by the BBC. Salford City co-owners Gary Neville and David Beckham. Salford City FC But after four promotions in five years, their progress stalled, and the ‘Ammies’ - a nickname taken from the club’s old name, Salford Amateurs - have been stuck in League Two for the past seven seasons. Most of the former players sold up as part of a recent ownership restructure which brought in fresh international capital - but Beckham and Gary Neville retained their shares, and their new ambition is to eventually bring Salford City into the Premier League.

Advertisement

The club has also gone back to its roots, reverting to its traditional orange colours this season and ditching the United-inspired red shirts introduced by the ex-players - a decision Gary Neville has since admitted was “quite selfish” and an error he was happy to rectify. League Two was not exactly top of Cklamovski’s list for his next job, but when the opportunity to join Salford City bobbed up while on holiday in England with his family, and he came to understand the scale of their project, he couldn’t say no. The initial approach was made by Gavin Fleig, a former City Football Group executive who now runs Salford City, and who knew Cklamovski from his time working under Postecoglou at Yokohama F. Marinos, a CFG partner club. Cklamovski, 48, was Postecoglou’s assistant in a variety of roles for more than a decade, but branched out on his own after lifting the Japanese title with Yokohama in 2019, and most recently was coach of the Malaysian national team.

Advertisement

Scholes no longer holds his 10 per cent stake, but remains at the club as chief football advisor. He was not alone in needing to look up Cklamovski’s name, but was blown away by his interview. “Peter was very impressive, right from the word go,” he said in a club feature on YouTube. Salford City chief football advisor Paul Scholes and coach Peter Cklamovski. Salford City FC Now Scholes watches the first team train most days, and acts as a valuable sounding board for Cklamovski. “He’s around for anything I need, really ... a really good eye for League Two because he’s been watching it for a decade or so, intimately,” Cklamovski says. “For me, that’s a depth of knowledge that I can always lean on.”

Advertisement

Other ex-United legends, including Roy Keane, routinely turn up for matches at their 2,246-seat home ground, Moor Lane, and more will jump on the bandwagon if their current form continues. After their most recent performance, a 4-2 victory over previously unbeaten Walsall, Gary Neville said he’d never seen Salford City play better football. With all the star power surrounding him, Cklamovski has to keep a deliberately narrow focus. ‘That’s a depth of knowledge that I can always lean on.’ Peter Cklamovski on working with Paul Scholes “There might be a bit of glitz and glamour in and around the club, but if I take my eye off what’s the most important thing, which is to get the football right, then I’m not doing my job,” he says. “The club has lofty ambitions, that’s for sure, and it’s being met with a solid plan. My job here is to put the foundation of the football in place ... build that identity of football for Salford City and, along with that, push hard and achieve success and get the club stepping up the English pyramid.“

Advertisement

For Cklamovski, that means doing what he has always done: trusting the process, even when it may feel like the walls are closing in on him. After those three first-up defeats, a fourth beckoned, and questions about his future would have surely followed. Salford were at home to Newport County and absolutely dominating - they finished with 31 shots to 4 - but it was one of those games when the ball just wouldn’t go in. Naturally, they went down 1-0 in the 71st minute, conceding a freakish long-range goal in which their goalkeeper was lobbed from 60 metres out. Peter Cklamovski. Getty Images “I’m thinking, ‘Oh no, not this again,’” Cklamovski says. “But there was a part inside me that was loving it. Seen it before, lived it before. I just knew that this is going to add to the story.”

Advertisement

Salford scored twice in the final 10 minutes, including a 90th-minute winner to prevail 2-1. Cklamovski looks back on it as the “circuit breaker” moment when his players were rewarded for refusing to abandon their principles - a familiar juncture for teams schooled in the ways of Angeball. Related Article Opinion

England The Ballon d’Or is everything football shouldn’t be. Thank goodness for Harry Kane Vince Rugari Reporter “I knew we were on track,” Cklamovski says. “I knew the boys were believing in the football, that the evidence was there on the pitch. They felt it. They saw it. They trained it.” The wins have flowed freely ever since, but there will be potholes in the road ahead. Cklamovski is encountering all the unique challenges of England’s lower professional leagues: the physicality is high, the stadiums almost uncomfortably intimate, the supporters fiercely passionate, while games can descend into disorder without warning. “There can be a lot of chaos in a game,” he says.

Advertisement

“It might be a referee call, it might be a tough away game, and the crowd get on top of you ... but chaos can get created very easily in this league. If we can control that chaos and play our football, then that control becomes a bit of a weapon.” It’s been a major change of pace for Cklamovski, who was accustomed to coaching in front of huge crowds in high-profile gigs in charge of FC Tokyo and Malaysia. Now he’s criss-crossing the heartlands of English football, working out of tiny grounds and falling for the peculiar romance of the lower leagues - all while trying to build something that he believes will one day find its way to a much bigger stage. “It’s humble beginnings right now,” he says. “But I’m sure in 12 months, 18 months, two years’ time - whether I’m here or not - the club will be a bigger brand, a bigger football club. You’ll see this place in a really innovative sort of spot where it’s building, and building something special. To be a small part of that, mate, it’s exciting.”

After a post-pandemic dip, Perth Festival is back doing what patrons want it to do: deliver the best in international arts and culture. Even though it’s been six years since COVID shut the world down, it has taken that long for the international arts touring scene to get back on track and for Perth Festival to be once again on global touring itineraries. Perth Festival artistic director Anna Reece. Frances Andrijich During that period, successive Perth Festival artistic directors have been forced to call upon local companies and artists to make up the numbers. While it has provided opportunities for local practitioners, it also led to a rumbling among patrons, who complained the city’s premier arts festival was not doing its job.

Advertisement

That longing for large-scale world-class works will be satisfied in 2027, which will be a series of European blockbuster shows that hark back to Perth Festival’s glory days, such as Peter Brook’s nine-hour Mahabharata in the Boya Quarry (back in 1988), and Robert Lepage’s Seven Streams of the River Ota in 1998, transformative experiences that still burn bright in the memory. “Perth deserves to experience some of the best, most exciting artists and ideas from around the world.” Perth Festival artistic director Anna Reece From Latvia comes trailblazing Polish director Łukasz Twarkowski’s ROTHKO, a four-hour time-shifting collision of cinema and theatre inspired by a famous art forgery; from Denmark comes Operation: Orfeo, a “hypnotic reimagining of the Greek myth of Orpheus and Eurydice told through extraordinary voices, light, architecture and illusion”; and from Greece comes Taverna Miresia – Mario, Bella, Anastasia, Mario Banushi’s wordless and visually stunning evocation of his Albanian childhood that recently won the Golden Lion at the Venice Biennale. Perth Festival artistic director Anna Reece was unapologetic about the pivot to the international for next year’s late-summer arts jamboree. “We are an international arts festival, and we should be proud of that. It is also our point of difference within the local scene,” Reece said ahead of Thursday’s program unveiling at the East Perth Power Station, which the Festival has brought back from the dead in the past two years.

Advertisement

“Over the past couple of years we’ve worked really hard to create a distinct identity for Perth Festival. “We have created new spaces for Perth people to gather and experience art, such as the Power Station and The Embassy Ballroom in the Perth Town Hall. Perth Festival will again take over the East Perth Power Station this year. Jessica Wyld Photography “These are now familiar gathering points that are critical for the Festival. “With those foundations in place we are ready to expand our international ambition again. Perth deserves to experience some of the best, most exciting artists and ideas from around the world.”

Advertisement

Reece said Perth Festival’s re-embracing of its international ambition, upon which it built its reputation, did not mean local practitioners would be overlooked. Editor's pick Marine life Where have the calves gone? The troubling shift in Australia’s whale highways “A great international arts festival should expand our sense of what’s possible at the same time as strengthening our commitment to WA artists. The two make each other stronger,” she said. “There were a number of local commissions last year and there will be another wave 2028. “It has to do with the cycles and the time it takes to complete work.

Advertisement

“International work challenges us and it challenges our local artists. It broadens our perspective and connects our city to conversations happening far beyond our borders.” Reece is reluctant to dive back into COVID – “it’s boring,” she laughs – but emphasised the damage the pandemic did to arts festivals around the world. Łukasz Twarkowski’s ROTHKO. “The knock-on effect of COVID has been enormous,” she said. “Everything stopped. It meant you couldn’t tap into the tours of European companies.

Advertisement

“If you wanted the work, they had to come back together and rehearse it. The global pipeline dried up. “Perth Festival over the years has hosted some of the great masters, such as Robert Lepage. This year we are introducing local audiences to the next generation of superstars, such as Łukasz Twarkowski and Mario Banushi. It’s incredibly exciting.” Perth Festival runs from February 5 to 28. Tickets for all shows are on sale from November 2. Lotterywest Films begins on November 23 with Jesse Eisenberg’s The Debut.

Victor Radley is eager to strike a new deal with the Roosters, but has conceded that he will entertain offers from NRL rivals – and even the Super League – for the first time in his career so he can look after his young family. Amid the exodus of stars including Mark Nawaqanitawase, Daly Cherry-Evans, Angus Crichton and Spencer Leniu that followed the Roosters’ premiership win, and this week’s headlines surrounding Sam Walker’s messy contract situation, it is easy to forget Radley will hit the open market for the first time on Sunday. Victor Radley trains with the England team in Wollongong on Thursday. Peter Keleman/SWpix.com The 28-year-old enforcer has spent a decade in the NRL, winning three premierships with the Roosters, and has never felt the need to explore what might be out there beyond the eastern suburbs – until now. Radley is in no rush to sort his future as he finalises his departure from long-time agent Sam Ayoub before joining a new management team.

The hard-hitting forward’s preference is to finish a one-club player, but said it was important his next contract was one that looked after his fiancée Taylah and two young boys, Vinnie and Cruze. If Radley, a local junior, cannot agree to a new deal with the Roosters, he is open to linking with an NRL rival – including the PNG Chiefs – or even a move to England, the country he will represent in the World Cup on Friday night against Papua New Guinea in Wollongong. I love new experiences, that might even include living in England and playing in the Super League. It’s something I’d be interested in.” Radley’s immediate focus, though, is finalising his management situation. “I’m joining a new company run by my fiancée’s uncle [Paul Williams] who has brought on board my good friend Max Muddle. London/Nassau: King Charles danced in the street with a troupe of dancers in the Bahamas on Wednesday, the second day of a royal visit to the Caribbean that has been somewhat overshadowed by increasingly vocal demands for Britain to pay reparations for its role in the slave trade. Wielding a pair of cowbells in the colours of the flag of the Bahamas, Charles took part in a traditional Junkanoo – a carnival event celebrating the island’s culture. King Charles shakes traditional cowbells at the head of the Bahamian Junkanoo. AP Dressed in a suit and sunglasses, the King cut a dapper figure at the front of the parade among the feathered headdresses and colourful costumes of the dancers, and was met with cheers by the crowd. He began the day by paying respects to fallen members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force, laying a wreath at the Flamingo Monument, and later visited the Bahamas Boxing Academy, where he was presented with a T-shirt bearing an image of himself wearing a champion’s belt.

Advertisement

Loading Arriving in the Bahamas on Tuesday for his first visit as King, Charles acknowledged the injustices of slavery, saying Commonwealth leaders would discuss the issue at their summit next week. Charles meets a young boxer at the Bahamas Boxing Academy in Nassau. Getty Images Speaking in the Bahamian capital Nassau at the start of a three-day trip, the King said it was “only right” to acknowledge “the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond”. Charles added that some of what was “best” in Bahamian culture today – “the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright” – was “born out of darkness”.

Advertisement

His remarks come before the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda next week, where regional leaders are expected to press demands for reparations for slavery and colonialism. Jamaica recently took its claim for reparations to Charles, and the case has since been referred to the UK’s highest court of appeal for the Caribbean island. The British government, however, has consistently rejected demands for either an apology or reparations. ‘Pay us what you owe us’ In Nassau, members of the islands’ Rastafarian community and others staged a demonstration near Clifford Park, where the King met local students, demanding reparations. “Pay us what you owe us!” one woman cried out. “I stand in memory of the horrors and the atrocities committed against black people.” Members of the Ethiopian African Black International Congress stage a demonstration in downtown Nassau. AP

Advertisement

Charles will visit Guyana next before travelling to Antigua and Barbuda where he will be joined by his wife, Queen Camilla, for the biennial summit of the Commonwealth which comprises 56 nations, mostly former British colonies. Related Article Analysis

International affairs King underlines peacemaker role as row hangs over Commonwealth summit The issue of reparations has gathered momentum across the Caribbean recently. Last month, CARICOM, the regional bloc, said it wanted the matter on the agenda at the summit. “The Caribbean has consistently asserted that reparations is fundamentally about justice,” CARICOM Secretary-General Carla Barnett said last month. Buckingham Palace had indicated that the King would address the issue during the tour, but not offer a formal apology, in line with British government policy, which also rules out financial reparations.

Advertisement

Charles inspects an honour guard of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force. AP A palace spokesperson said the visit would focus mainly on “modern partnerships and opportunities for the future” in the region, but added that for Charles it was also part of “a lifelong” effort to engage with and educate about “the most shameful aspects of our past”. Campaigners and some Caribbean leaders have called on Britain to go further, including through an apology, reparations in the form of financial compensation and the return of cultural artefacts. From the 15th to the 19th century, at least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into slavery by European traders, with Britain transporting an estimated 3.2 million people across the Atlantic, making it one of the biggest slave-trading nations. title: Consumers are mincemeat, but the RBA keeps raising the heat

If you hadn’t guessed already, Australia’s top retailers can confirm we’re all doing it pretty tough at the moment. On Wednesday, Woolies boss Amanda Bardwell told investors that despite a drop in the average price of the supermarket’s groceries, customers are shopping around more keenly than ever and only showing loyalty to the cheapest deal. Prices are going up and up, and so are interest rates. Louie Douvis “The amount of pressure on young families, particularly, and families more broadly is increasing,” Bardwell says. Mince has never been more popular – Woolies’ sales are up significantly – as families try to keep their bellies full on cheaper protein.

Advertisement

It looks like the soaring price of lamb chops and steak will be the proverbial barbecue stopper this summer. But it’s more sobering than that, with the news this week that food insecurity is a reality in middle-income families. One in three households are going hungry as the cost-of-living crisis bites, a Foodbank survey has found. Related Article Analysis

Inflation Grant Theft warning: Chalmers faces new inflation nightmare before Christmas And don’t expect this pressure to ease. El Nino is adding to the risk of even higher food prices, with reduced rainfall and higher temperatures expected to hit livestock and crop production. But the price shock doesn’t stop at the kitchen table.

Advertisement

On Thursday, shopping bellwethers JB Hi-Fi, Rebel sports chain owner Super Retail and Bunnings joined the chorus of retailers pointing to the impact of the cost-of-living crisis on their sales. Preparations for festive season bargain hunting may have helped send sales into reverse in the September quarter at JB Hi-Fi’s electronic retail franchise in Australia. “The group continues to see variability in trading and heightened competitive activity, with customers remaining focused on value and increasingly shopping during promotional events,” chief executive Nick Wells told investors at its annual meeting. RBA Governor Michele Bullock looks set to announce yet another rate hike next week. Louise Kennerley “In October, the group has seen sales slow ahead of the important Black Friday and Christmas trading periods.”

Advertisement

Even Wesfarmers’ rock star businesses Bunnings and Kmart are feeling the pain from shoppers’ constraint. Wesfarmers boss Rob Scott told his fellow shareholders in Perth how “persistent cost pressures with elevated inflation and rising interest rates” have created a moderation in retail demand. He said the group had noted at its full-year results in August how the uncertain outlook for inflation, house prices, interest rates and tax settings were weighing on consumer sentiment. Since then, the Reserve Bank has lifted rates yet again, and a fifth rate hike for the year is expected on Melbourne Cup Day. It will only worsen the pressure on household and business budgets. Add in a shock inflation result this week, and the only question is how much worse is it about to get. Some economists are already forecasting that a rate rise next week may not be the last, after the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported inflation climbed to a higher-than-expected 4.3 per cent in September.

Advertisement

US President Donald Trump’s war in the Middle East continues to send energy prices much higher than the RBA had assumed in August. RBA Governor Michele Bullock also pointed to the equally unyielding AI boom, which is driving up computer chip and storage costs and is adding to a global construction boom. Bullock told a Senate committee this week that Australia’s labour market is “a little tighter than we had previously judged”, despite rising unemployment. That’s right, the working poor are part of the problem.

Advertisement

An interesting aside to the soaring inflation rate is that it includes a rapid rise in the price in legitimate tobacco sales from a higher excise, but overlooks the massive decline in real dollars spent on cigarettes as smokers move almost entirely to the black market. Related Article Opinion

Tax reform On the day that ‘stops the nation’, the RBA will stop inflation (again) Ross Gittins Economics Editor It would be comical, if not for the further pressure it puts on non-smoking families via higher inflation, which is prompting higher interest rates. What to do? Peace in the Middle East would help ease the searing pain for Australian households.

Advertisement

So would an AI crash that knocks out the soaring cost of expensive tech components – though it could spark another global financial crisis, with dire consequences for companies, and, ultimately, consumers. As far as local concerns go, our productivity needs to do some heavy lifting too, as departing Wesfarmers chairman Mike Chaney points out. “Our economy is facing headwinds – low growth, weak productivity, dismal confidence and limited ambition or capacity for reform,” he outlined in an interview this week. Lots of ingredients in this toxic mix. And none of it is going to be fixed at the kitchen table. The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

title: Massive Keralup gas plant could power neighbouring data centre
text:

Western Australia’s biggest-ever proposed gas-fired power plant could power a neighbouring data centre, but the energy infrastructure giant behind the plan has stressed no agreements have been signed yet. APA Group’s Keralup power station, 53 kilometres south of Perth, is currently open for public comment by the Environmental Protection Authority. APA’s Keralup Energy Hub. According to documents lodged with the EPA, the 870-megawatt, gas-fired power station will be split into a 210-megawatt temporary facility providing electricity solely for an “industrial client”, and a separate 660 megawatt facility that will feed into the South West power grid, as well as a large grid-scale battery system. WAtoday understands a major data centre builder has expressed interest in a nearby site in the future Keralup industrial area, though no plans have been lodged.

Advertisement

When asked about the mystery client, APA said no agreements had been signed with any client, but the company’s group executive of energy solutions confirmed data centres would make a good customer for the power plant. “APA has not executed agreements with any customer for the offtake of the energy associated with this potential development,” Rogers said. “APA is progressing planning and approvals for the site to ensure we are ready to support potential future customers, which is our standard approach and occurring at multiple sites across the country. “The site has the potential to provide grid firming to the South-West Interconnected System and directly support industrial energy users, including data centres, having been identified for decades as a potential industrial development site by successive state governments. “The site is unsuitable for residential development, is located away from residential areas and is close to existing enabling infrastructure.”

Advertisement

The temporary 210 megawatt facility will run from 2027 for three to five years. Related Article Updated

Gas Mystery client drives plans for WA’s biggest gas power station amid green push APA Group has previously expressed interest in powering data centres. In an interview with Livewire in February, APA Group chief executive Adam Watson said the company was exploring behind-the-grid power plants similar to those used in mining operations. “Data centres consume an enormous amount of energy … and quite frankly, there’s just not enough power available on the grid,” he told the website.

Advertisement

“Think of a solution where you’ve got an industrial park where we could build a gas-fired power generator, a solar farm, a battery, and be able to have that data centre operate on that piece of land. “Could be a really interesting one to watch.” The prospect of a gas-powered data centre in Keralup has concerned the WA Greens, who want the Cook government to rule it out. “There’s zero way that in 2026 we can allow this carbon bomb to proceed,” Greens fossil fuels and climate change spokeswoman Sophie McNeill said. “Is the Cook government reneging on their commitment to the federal plan for new data centres to be powered by renewable energy?

Advertisement

“It is simply not acceptable to claim that you want to be a renewable energy powerhouse one day and then the same week, entertain the building of the largest new gas-fired power station in Western Australian history.” Related Article Data centres The two WA regions where the world’s AI companies want to build data centres Earlier this week, the Cook government announced it would set a renewable energy target on the South West power gride from 40 per cent this year to 75 per cent by 2031. On Tuesday, Energy Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said the Keralup facility was a private project. The Cook government has kept an open mind about data centres, with the premier last month suggesting the Mid West and North West regions of the state would make ideal locations for the mammoth facilities driving the AI boom.

Advertisement

According to APA documents, the new power station will burn through about 150 terajoules per day, which is about 10 per cent of the state’s current daily use. When fully operational, the facility will produce more than 3 million tonnes of carbon annually. The prospect of large-scale data centres, particularly near metropolitan Perth, has been met with fierce opposition from local communities. Five months after GreenSquareDC was forced to withdraw its application for a $600 million data centre near the banks of the Helena River due to public outcry, a Canberra-based developer hopes to have more luck. Canberra Data Centres (CDC) is looking to build a $337 million four-storey centre at 178 and 196 Bushmead Road around two kilometres from the proposed GreenSquareDC site.

Advertisement

The development would take up 85,945 square metres and comprise 87 parking bays.

Warwick Farm trainer Bjorn Baker hopes a kind draw can prove the difference for perennial bridesmaid Within The Law when she looks to build off an impressive Silver Eagle finish in the $10 million Golden Eagle. Within The Law’s three career wins came across her first starts; in the Inglis Banner, Nursery and group 2 Sweet Embrace Stakes. She fell next time out in the Golden Slipper before placings in the Percy Sykes, Silver Shadow, Champagne and Flight Stakes, as well as the Fred Best and Gunsynd Classics. Within The Law​, (centre pink cap), winning the Inglis Nursery in December 2024. Getty Images Baker tested her Golden Eagle credentials first-up in the 1300m Silver Eagle, where she surged down the inside to finish less than a length away in fifth on a day jockeys were avoiding that part of the track. Drawn in gate seven that day, Within The Law has barrier three for the Golden Eagle, where Rachel King rides the $34 hope.

Advertisement

Baker, who was unlucky in the Golden Eagle with Stefi Magnetica in 2024, hoped the fast-finisher could defy the odds. “It’s a tough race, but she was really good first up,” Baker said. “It’s the sort of race you need a little bit of luck in, and we were hoping for that and the key was that she’s drawn a gate. That’s a big help. “She’s been a great horse. At the end of the day, she’s won nearly $2 million, is a group 2 winner and is often thereabouts. Second in the Flight Stakes and the Champagne, so we know she’s good around that mile mark at Randwick, and she had a bit of residual fitness from Brisbane. Within The Law, left, comes with a late run in the Silver Eagle. Getty Images

Advertisement

“It’s a tough race, we’re under no illusions, but they will go quick enough to give her a chance.” Baker also has Pericles and Caballus set to contest the $3 million Russell Balding Stakes (1300m). Caballus, a surprise call-up for the Everest, was two and a half lengths away in seventh in the $20 million race last start as a $151 outsider. He was $12 for Saturday after drawing gate one. Pericles, who was also an acceptor at Flemington, appeared likely to run at Randwick. He was $18 from gate two after finishing two and a quarter lengths off last time out in the Everest consolation race. “Both of them have got good gates and they are both going really well,” Baker said.

Advertisement

“Caballus was excellent in the Everest and with any luck he might have finished a bit closer. The key is we’ve got a really good gate, gate one, good track. I think he’s definitely a live chance. “And if Pericles goes there, he’s definitely not out of it. His run in the Sydney Stakes was excellent after having to cover a heap of ground. He looks fantastic now.” At Flemington, Baker hoped Paradoxium ($17) could bounce back in the group 1 Coolmore Stud Stakes (1200m) after a fading fourth in the Roman Consul Stakes. “He probably overdid it, but he still ran a good race. Fourth in a group 2 and it’s a good form race to go to the Coolmore,” he said. “He’s a lovely colt and we’ve been thrilled with him since. He’s done everything really well and he’s not out of it.”

Baker, meanwhile, was into the Melbourne Cup with So You Are on Thursday after he received a one-kilogram penalty for Wednesday’s Bendigo Cup win. The penalty lifted So You Are to 24th in the order of entry after Ciaron Maher-trained Saint George failed its mandatory scan. Tulloch Lodge’s The Euphrates was also ahead in the order but co-trainer Adrian Bott confirmed he was not racing on after 10ths in the Geelong and Bendigo Cups.

The AFL has crowned Sydney as the primetime kings, with the Swans set to face their former star Nick Blakey in a highly anticipated grudge match in round eight, as the full 2027 fixture was released on Thursday. New Hawk Zach Merrett won’t have to wait long to face his former side Essendon, where he had been captain and claimed seven best and fairests, with a clash between Hawthorn and the Bombers scheduled for the Saturday night of round three (April 3) at the MCG. Big games against former clubs in 2027: (from left) Western Bulldog Zak Butters, Hawthorn’s Zach Merrett and North Melbourne’s Nick Blakey. AFL Photos, Getty Images. Artwork: The Age Sydney – whose 2026 season ended in controversy after the Pullman hotel incident, into which there is an ongoing police investigation – will appear in seven Friday night timeslots and two Thursday nights across the first 16 rounds. Hawthorn, Adelaide and Geelong also claimed several primetime spots, with the Hawks and Crows snagging four Friday night slots while the Cats claimed three.

Advertisement

The Swans will face their former teammate Blakey – who left Sydney under frosty conditions and joined North Melbourne on a multimillion-dollar contract – in a clash at the SCG on May 8. Blakey is one of five Sydney players handed season-ending suspensions by the club for their part in a wild night of partying in August. A separate Victoria Police investigation is ongoing after three women, working as exotic dancers, variously alleged they were sexually assaulted and touched inappropriately without consent. No charges have been laid, and the investigation is ongoing into four players (Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Blakey), with one (Riley Bice) being treated as a witness. The players have denied the allegations. Similar to 2026, Collingwood have retained their primetime spots, claiming three Thursday night games and three Friday night games.

title: A familiar political crisis could be looming as Israel counts its votes
text:
In brief Israel voted five times in less than four years between 2019 and 2022, as alliances repeatedly fell apart.

Neither side currently has a clear path to a majority - uncomfortable deals and potential deadlock could follow.

Israel has just voted, but the country could face another election within months if its deeply divided political parties fail to negotiate alliances to form a new government.

Israelis know this scenario all too well. Between 2019 and 2022, the country held five elections in less than four years, as coalitions repeatedly struggled to assemble majorities or fell apart once they did.

With around 90 per cent of votes from Wednesday's election counted, neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, have enough seats in their coalitions to assemble a majority.

Netanyahu's bloc is projected to win 53 seats, while Eisenkot's opposition is set for 48, though these figures may still change. The threshold for a majority is 61.

Meanwhile, two Arab parties — the Joint List and Ra'am — are on course for a historic combined 19 seats, potentially handing them significant influence over who forms the next government. But neither side has expressed willingness to work with them, limiting the Jewish blocs' paths to a majority.
