"Maybe everybody lost in these elections but the Arab parties. And for the Arab parties, it's unclear that they can make use of their huge success," Hebrew University of Jerusalem political scientist Gideon Rahat said.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog is now tasked with choosing a leader with the best chance of forming a government, with input from each party.

"We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections," he said after early results arrived, urging parties to keep "an open mind".

Israeli politics is known for its twists, turns and unlikely alliances, and many different scenarios could play out in the weeks to come — including a very real possibility of a stalemate that could take months to resolve.

So what happens if neither side can form a government?

The struggle to govern Israel

No party has ever won enough seats to govern Israel alone, forcing leaders to negotiate alliances with other parties.

Eisenkot faces particularly difficult choices, including the prospect of working with Netanyahu in a unity government, or with Arab parties, both of which he said he would not do.

His bloc includes both right-wing parties and the left-wing Democrats, the only Jewish party open to partnering with Arab-led parties.

Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen has indicated he would support an opposition government to oust Netanyahu without formally joining it, potentially opening the door to a fragile minority government.

But working with Arab parties could cost Eisenkot the support of right-wing allies, leaving him with few straightforward paths to power.

Netanyahu's options for partnerships appear more limited. Neither the Arab parties nor any of those in the opposition bloc have expressed willingness to work with him, though in Israeli politics, it's never wise to say never.

"As they say, politics is the art of the possible. In Israeli politics, it's the art of the unimaginable," Ran Porat, an Israel and Middle East lecturer and analyst at Monash University, told SBS News.

A stalemate could benefit Netanyahu

A prolonged political deadlock could work in Netanyahu's favour, allowing him to remain caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed.

That prospect has raised questions about how he might use his powers in the interim, particularly amid speculation over a renewed Israeli attack on Iran.

In the days leading up to the election, Netanyahu called for the overthrow of Iran's government. Media reports, which he denied, suggested senior military officials had pushed back against his plans to strike Iran ahead of the vote.

Following the election, Eisenkot warned Israel's security chiefs against allowing Netanyahu to put his political survival ahead of the national interest.

Porat says another deadlock could also result in lower turnout in a future election, disillusioning voters who turned out in force for this vote.

"The side that is anti-Netanyahu, the Arab sector, and the liberals, will be much less motivated to go and vote after they made this enormous effort this time around and did not reach a victory," he said.

Israel has been here before

In the April 2019 election, Netanyahu's party tied with the Blue and White alliance led by Benny Gantz, both securing 35 seats.

But efforts to form a government failed amid disagreements over military conscription exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Jews, triggering another election in September.

That vote also failed to produce a government.

A third election in March 2020 eventually resulted in a unity government between Gantz and Netanyahu who agreed to share the prime ministership on a rotating basis.

That government collapsed after less than a year over a budget dispute, before Gantz could take his turn as leader, prompting a fourth election in March 2021.

That vote produced an unlikely eight-party coalition spanning the political spectrum — including an Arab Islamist party for the first time — bring Netanyahu's premiership to an end.

The government was led initially by the right-wing Naftali Bennett and later the centrist Yair Lapid under a power-sharing agreement. But the coalition struggled to reconcile its ideological differences and lost its majority.

Its collapse saw Lapid take over as caretaker prime minister ahead of a fifth election in November 2022, which returned Netanyahu to power.

Lessons for Eisenkot

Porat says the lessons from the last political crisis "have been internalised [by Eisenkot] quite significantly".

He said the collapse of the previous anti-Netanyahu coalition highlighted the importance of party loyalty over ideology, after several right-wing politicians broke ranks, leading to the breakdown of the government.

"So the first lesson is to get people who are loyal to you, which they did, on Eisenkot's side," he said.

The second lesson, he added, is to avoid addressing how to resolve issues with Palestinians, particularly in the West Bank.

"Because if there's something that all parties disagree about ... is what should be done with the settlements and possibly future annexation or compromise."

That issue is "toxic" for the anti-Netanyahu bloc, he explained, particularly if it ultimately ends up including an Arab party.

Views across such a coalition could range anywhere from calling for an immediate two-state solution to annexing the West Bank.

Eisenkot has been cautious about articulating a long-term vision for Palestinians during his campaign, though he has rejected the prospect of a two-state solution under current conditions while opposing Israeli annexation of the occupied West Bank.

Many analysts say it's unlikely, even under a new government, that there will be any significant progress towards territorial compromises with Palestinians in the immediate future.

"Avoid that [issue] at all costs, because that will break down the government," Porat said.

— With additional reporting by Agence France-Presse.

title: How a Kylian Mbappé 'dictator' meme prompted a Real Madrid apology to China
text:
In brief French footballer Kylian Mbappé and Real Madrid apologised after comments about Mao Zedong sparked backlash in China.

Chinese broadcasters and sponsors cut ties as outrage over the remarks spread online.

Real Madrid has apologised to China after star striker Kylian Mbappé apparently joked about Mao Zedong in comments that sparked a social media storm and saw Spanish football yanked off state TV.

Mocking former leader Mao — blamed by historians for millions of deaths — is taboo in China, and Mbappé's remarks saw him become the latest foreign sports figure to anger the country.

In a clip of a video interview with French show The Bridge — since taken down — Mbappé talked about being amused by an internet meme of his face photo-shopped onto "some guy, think he's a Chinese dictator", an apparent reference to Mao.

The fallout was immediate. Chinese beverage giant Dongpeng, which during this year's World Cup ran adverts with AI-generated images of Mbappé, said on Tuesday it had scrapped its partnership with the player, as did dairy firms Mengniu and Milkground.

CMG, which oversees public broadcaster CCTV, said it had suspended broadcasts of La Liga, the world's second-richest football league after England's Premier League.

On Wednesday, Real Madrid issued a statement saying it "wishes to express its apologies to the Chinese people for any offence caused by the recent remarks of our player Kylian Mbappé".

"The club joins in the public apology issued by Kylian Mbappé, in which the player himself expressed his regret for his words and reiterated his respect for the Chinese people," the 15-time European champions said.

The statement came a day after Mbappé — who was the top scorer in this year's World Cup with 10 goals — issued his own apology, saying: "My comment was ill-judged and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world."

Mbappé made the comments while speaking with French show The Bridge. Source: Supplied

Foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a regular briefing on Wednesday: "We take seriously the apology the individual concerned has made."

La Liga said on Tuesday it "deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé's recent comments have caused among Chinese fans".

Earlier, the Chinese state-run Global Times said in an editorial that it was "not difficult to see that the club's longstanding tolerance of such behaviour has contributed to Mbappé's latest offensive remarks".

Mbappé, 27, continued to face a torrent of criticism from Chinese web users on Wednesday, some of it racist.

"His remarks were hurtful toward China and the Chinese people, so they cannot be translated," wrote one user on social media platform Weibo.

Mbappé's original joke about Mao was not reposted — or had been scrubbed — from China's tightly controlled social media.

Drinks company Dongpeng was among the Chinese companies to cut ties with Kylian Mbappé. Source: Getty / Liu Junfeng

Chinese social media app Xiaohongshu had meanwhile frozen Mbappé's account, where he has over a million followers.

The same was done on the Weibo app, with a notice stating that "the user has been banned from following due to violating laws or the Weibo Community Convention".

Some Chinese media reports said global brands like Dior and Hublot had removed their Mbappé-related content on Weibo.

A search by the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency on Dior and Hublot's Weibo page with Mbappé's Chinese name produced no results.

'Respect history'

Offline too the Mbappé brand appeared to be under threat.

When AFP visited the Adidas flagship store in Beijing's Sanlitun shopping district, Real Madrid shirts were available for sale, but none bearing the striker's name.

Chinese state media have previously praised Mbappé as a "footballing sensation" and "talent".

His face is plastered on billboards, on soft drinks and across social media.

Kylian Mbappé had sponsorship deals with several Chinese companies that have scrapped the agreements following the controversy. Source: Getty / Future Publishing

Mbappé is sometimes affectionately referred to as "Guigui", meaning "turtle" in Chinese, for his resemblance to a character from the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles movie.

Other major overseas sports leagues have previously angered China.

China suspended sponsorship deals with the US National Basketball Association while the state broadcaster pulled NBA games off Chinese television for a year in October 2019.

This followed Houston Rockets executive Daryl Morey tweeting "Fight for freedom, stand with Hong Kong", referring to protests the Chinese government called separatist and seditious.

"Respecting the history, culture, social customs and national sentiments of others is a fundamental principle for cross-border interaction, a standard of conduct widely upheld by the international community," the official People's Daily newspaper said in an opinion piece.

title: Australia's $550 fuel hit is among world's highest
text:
In brief Australians have paid more than $500 extra for fuel amid the global fuel crisis.

Experts say that industry is driving Australia's reliance on diesel.

Surging fuel prices amid the war in the Middle East have cost Australians more than $500 per person on average, with the national impact of fuel price shocks exceeding $14 billion since March this year according to a report.

Australians have seen the third-highest fuel price increases compared to other countries, with individuals paying on average $546 more than usual, according to analysis from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).

The analysis, which compared average fuel prices in January to February, before the disruption of shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, with prices during March to October, found that price shocks had cost 169 countries, including Australia, $665 billion.

The country paying the most amid global fuel shocks was the United States, with more than $226 billion in additional costs.

Americans paid an extra $666 per person, Canadians $597, and New Zealand's motorists followed close behind Australians at $484 per person.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Senior economist at the University of Sydney Luke Hartigan said Australia's position in the top four alongside Canada, the US and New Zealand made sense, considering Australia has the highest per capita diesel usage rates in the world, driven by high use in mining and farming.

"That's why similar patterns appear in the US, Canada and New Zealand, all of which have large agricultural sectors, and Canada also has a significant mining industry," Hartigan told SBS News.

Australia was among the top three countries for fuel expenditure per person, with the bulk of the cost coming from diesel. Source: SBS News / CREA

Geography was also an important factor, he said.

"Apart from New Zealand, these countries are vast, and distances between production centres and consumers are enormous."

"Moving fruit and vegetables from Queensland to Sydney, or freight from the Northern Territory to major cities, can involve distances comparable to crossing Europe."

Diesel costs blow out

Australia imports more than 90 per cent of its refined and crude oil, leaving it particularly vulnerable to fuel price shocks amid ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

But another issue contributing to Australia's vulnerability was its increasing use of diesel, which Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) CEO Amandine Denis-Ryan said was "really at odds" with the rest of the world.

"Between 2000 and recent years, Australia increased its diesel intensity by 33 per cent, while the world decreased it by 30 per cent, and countries like the US and Japan reduced it by 50 per cent," she told SBS News.

As the world's largest importer of diesel, Australia represents 10 per cent of the global seaborne diesel trade and is also the third-largest importer of petrol and jet fuel.

When compared with Australia's share of global GDP and population, Denis-Ryan said, "These numbers are enormous."

Australia paid almost $15 billion more for fuel from March to October. Source: SBS News / CREA

Diesel use has been trending upwards this century according to government figures, that show diesel comprises 44.1 per cent of transport energy use. It's the most used road and rail transport fuel and is a popular ship fuel.

"We've been shifting away from rail freight towards road freight, and we've also been shifting from underground coal mines, which mostly use electricity, to open-cut coal mines, which mostly use diesel," Denis-Ryan said.

And there are geological factors as well: "As we exhaust our best and most easily accessible mineral resources, we need more diesel for each tonne of coal produced and each tonne of ore produced," Denis-Ryan said, adding that Australia's vehicles were largely "really old and quite inefficient".

Australian households paying the price

Recent research from IEEFA assessed the link between inflation and oil shocks, and found that "in the last six inflation flare-ups in Australia since 2000, oil price shocks were a key contributor every time".

A reduction in the impact of oil price shocks on Australia's economy could provide broader economic benefits, Denis-Ryan said, noting that households would be less vulnerable to inflation if they switched to electric cars.

The CREA report found that while the US experienced enormous fuel costs, US electric vehicle (EV) drivers had seen just a $17 increase in charging costs since the start of March.

Hartigan said there has been an "enormous" uptake of EVs in Australia, starting at the height of the fuel crisis in March. Data from the National Australia Bank showed that EV loans doubled as Australians sought to dodge soaring petrol and diesel prices.

Senior economist at the left-wing thinktank the Australia Institute Matt Grudnoff said that governments could reduce or offset the upfront purchase cost of EVs.

But he said the bid to electrify Australia's roads should focus on industry.

"The public conversation tends to focus on household fuel costs because that's where people notice the impact most directly when they fill up their cars.

"But the data shows that a large share of the economic impact happens behind the scenes through freight and transport.

"Higher fuel prices increase the cost of moving goods around the country, which then contributes to inflation across the economy."

A move toward EVs

A recent report from the Climate Council found Australia paid more than twice as much as any other nation in additional diesel import costs during the global fuel crisis, putting the toll at $9 billion over six months.

Moves to renewable energy had saved Australians from some higher costs, the report found, with electric and hybrid cars cutting $1.7 billion in costs and saving the equivalent of 17.4 million litres of petrol and diesel per week.

Denis-Ryan said she hoped the fuel crisis would be a "wake-up call" for Australia, "particularly in terms of accelerating transport electrification, but also in looking at how we can slow the growth of oil use, and diesel use in particular, throughout Australia".

title: The $2.5 billion cancer bill Australia's sunscreen overhaul may not fix
text:
in brief The regulator is now developing reforms to strengthen sunscreen testing.

But experts say more reliable testing is only part of the solution.

Australia's sunscreen regulator is planning tougher rules after concerns some products failed to deliver the sun protection promised on their labels.

But experts say more reliable testing is only part of the solution, with boosting awareness on how Australians need to apply and reapply sunscreen also critical to preventing skin cancer.

In a report published last year, consumer group CHOICE tested 20 popular sunscreens and found that only four met their labelled sun protection factor (SPF), raising questions about the reliability of products Australians rely on to protect themselves from UV radiation.

The Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) later recalled several sunscreen products after identifying batches that didn't deliver their advertised SPF protection.

The regulator is now developing reforms to strengthen sunscreen testing, improve ingredient-quality requirements, and clarify the SPF claims cosmetic products can make.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

What are the proposed reforms?

The TGA is proposing several reforms to address sunscreen quality, with the goal of reducing instances of skin cancer.

Australia has the highest rate of melanoma incidence in the world, with an estimated 17,443 new cases diagnosed in 2025 according to Cancer Australia.

The reforms are:

Strengthen sunscreen testing requirements

Develop specific ingredient quality requirements

Provide a consistent limit for SPF rating that can be claimed for all secondary (cosmetic) sunscreens

Review sunscreen good manufacturing practice guidance

Consider labelling for SPF ratings

Professor Terry Slevin, CEO of the Public Health Association of Australia, told SBS News that treating skin cancers costs the country almost $2.5 billion each year.

"We need to invest more in preventing those cancers rather than having to treat them at the tail end," he said.

The TGA told SBS News: "The proposed reforms are intended to provide greater assurance through stronger testing requirements, increased oversight of testing laboratories, testing of finished products and periodic testing over a product’s lifecycle, and improved access by the TGA to SPF testing evidence."

Improving testing

Improving how sunscreen is tested is one way the TGA wants to improve quality and reliability of SPF claims.

Slevin explained that a small number of labs in Australia produce the nation's sunscreen, supplying multiple brands.

Sunscreens can then be tested on volunteers who use the formula and are then exposed to UV radiation; the rate at which skin reddens can then be used to determine the product's quality.

Experts say sunscreen safety is not just about the products, but also how we apply it. Source: AAP / Dan Himbrechts

While this method is common, it can also be imprecise.

"People have different skin types, and the amount of product being applied can vary a lot. So having consistent SPF levels relies on a lot of unpredictable variables," Slevin said.

These variations can lead to inconsistent product application and to sunscreens having marginally different SPF than advertised on their packaging.

Should you be worried about SPF levels?

The TGA reforms are looking to ensure that sunscreen manufacturers have clearer guidance and expectations, but SPF levels could still slightly vary from bottle to bottle according to Slevin.

However, variations would be minimal and would have little impact on the sunscreen's efficacy.

"The difference between SPF 50 and SPF 30 may sound significant, but the difference in the amount of UV that’s filtered out is only 3 per cent, a small change," he said.

"The vast majority of sunscreens serve a very useful and effective purpose; these reforms will only strengthen this."

But the main way to achieve the TGA's goal may not be reforming testing, but educating people on how to use sunscreen products best.

Dispelling confusion

Anna Wang, an associate professor in the School of Chemistry at UNSW Sydney, said that improving consumer understanding and behaviour is the best way to improve sun safety.

"What is going to make a bigger impact isn’t whether a sunscreen tests SPF45 using one method and SPF40 using another, but how often we reapply, and whether we put the recommended amount on," she told SBS News.

Experts recommended applying sunscreen generously to all exposed skin every two hours, seeking shade, and wearing a hat and sunglasses.

Towelling off after a swim, or wiping water or sweat off your body, can also remove some sunscreen.

Some cosmetic products, including foundations and moisturisers, also advertise SPF protection.

The TGA is considering a consistent limit on the SPF ratings these secondary sunscreens can claim, aiming to make it easier for consumers to distinguish products designed primarily for sun protection from those intended mainly for cosmetic use.

"In Australia, we have several hundred formulations to choose from so it can be confusing," Wang said.

She supported the TGA's reforms to clarify the distinction between primary and secondary sunscreens.

Investigation ongoing

In the meantime, the TGA confirmed to SBS News its investigation into sunscreens with disputed SPF results is ongoing.

"The TGA is considering the available evidence and providing sponsors with an opportunity to provide additional data or evidence before regulatory decisions are made," it told SBS News.

The regulator said it will issue product recalls or cancellations as needed while it develops the new reforms.

"The TGA intends to publish its findings and learnings and provide further guidance to sponsors and manufacturers to clarify expectations around SPF evidence and testing."

title: Inflation 'persisting longer' than desired, Treasurer says, after surprising spike
text:
In brief Core inflation rose faster than expected, adding to pressure on the Reserve Bank.

Fresh inflation data has fuelled expectations of another interest rate hike.

Core inflation climbed 1 per cent in Australia over the quarter, with the Reserve Bank governor warning underlying inflation is still too high.

The September quarter increase in the trimmed mean was in line with economists' expectations but exceeded the central bank's forecast of a 0.8 per cent increase.

On an annualised basis, the trimmed mean — a measure of underlying inflation that removes the biggest price swings — rose 3.6 per cent.

Headline inflation was hotter than expected by the market, at 1.3 per cent over the quarter.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers acknowledged inflation is persisting "longer than anyone would like" and citing the war in the Middle East as a major factor.

Markets had upped their bets for a November hike after comments in the past week by the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) deputy governor, Andrew Hauser, and chief economist Sarah Hunter, indicating that inflation remained too high.

At the same time as the data was published by the Australian Bureau of Statistics, RBA governor Michele Bullock was appearing alongside Hauser, Hunter and other top officials at a Senate estimates hearing.

Elevated underlying inflationary pressures were a sign that the labour market was still tight, Bullock said.

"The Monetary Policy Board will meet next week," she said.

"We'll discuss our assessment of the flow of data and how the risks are unfolding. A key question is whether the tightening in monetary policy to date will be sufficient to bring inflation back to target in a reasonable time."

Source: SBS News

Monthly headline inflation rose 4.3 per cent on an annual basis, up from 4 per cent in the 12 months to August.

"Housing was the largest contributor to annual inflation in September, rising by 5.2 per cent," said Rachael McCririck, ABS head of price statistics.

Transport was the second largest contributor, rising by 8.7 per cent annually, due to higher fuel costs.

Fuel and the war in the Middle East

Speaking to press in Canberra, Treasurer Jim Chalmers issued a small mea culpa.

"We accept our part in the fight against inflation," Chalmers said.

"We take responsibility for government policy when it comes to the fiscal settings and when it comes to managing the budget in a responsible way in the face of this inflation challenge, which is persisting longer than anyone would like."

Chalmers again blamed rising inflation on higher fuel prices driven by the conflict in the Middle East.

The penalty leaves Australia's biggest listed casino operator facing an uncertain future.

Australia's biggest listed casino company is on the brink of administration after being fined $260 million for historical money-laundering violations.

title: The $9 billion fuel bill raising questions about Australia's energy security
text:
In brief Australia paid a higher price for imported diesel than any other nation during the fuel crisis.

New analysis linked billions in extra fuel costs to energy security risks.

Australia has paid more than twice as much as any other nation in additional diesel import costs during the global fuel crisis, with a report putting the toll at $9 billion over six months.

The added cost equates to $324 for every Australian, exceeding the bills incurred by Brazil, South Africa, France and the UK.

The Climate Council released the figures from its energy security scorecard on Wednesday, which also found Australia paid an extra $1.6 billion for petrol imports.

The findings come days after oil prices reached a six-month high amid escalating threats in the Middle East.

The council's report, called Crude Awakening, analysed Australia's energy security, its exposure to rising global fuel prices, and policies and progress towards electric transport and renewable energy.

It found Australia was the world's largest seaborne importer of diesel, with imports responsible for 90 per cent of its supply.

Diesel use in Australia had also more than doubled since 2000 to 33 billion litres in 2025, with about a quarter used in mining.

title: More Australians are seeing a GP. What happens next is becoming more complex
text:
IN BRIEF Australian doctors are bridging gaps in the medical system as mental health presentations increase.

Longer consultation times are being driven by "increasingly complex" patient needs.

General practitioners (GPs) are spending more time with patients, treating increasingly complex conditions and working across specialist remits, according to a new report.

The Royal Australian College of GPs (RACGP) is calling on the federal government to increase Medicare patient rebates for longer consultations, after its latest Health of the Nation report found that two-thirds of GPs were spending more time with patients than in previous years.

In 2026, the average consultation length increased to 19.8 minutes per patient, up from 19.7 minutes in 2025 and 17.7 minutes in 2022.

Over 70 per cent of the 2,766 Australian GPs surveyed in the report identified increasingly complex care as their biggest issue — driven by growing rates of chronic disease, high rates of mental health presentations and an ageing population.

Psychological presentations were the leading reason patients sought care in 2025, reported by 67 per cent of practising GPs.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The figure has remained high over the past decade, rising from 61 per cent in 2017 to a high of 72 per cent in 2023 following the COVID-19 pandemic.

One GP quoted in the study said there had been a "marked rise" in anxiety, depression, trauma-related disorders and social isolation across all age groups, especially among young adults and working-age populations.

"Many presentations are linked to financial stress, housing insecurity, workplace pressures, and relationship breakdowns rather than purely medical causes."

The range of reasons GPs are spending more time with patients is wide and varied. Source: SBS News

More patients were presenting with complex psycho-social needs, requiring longer consultations, continuity of care, and multidisciplinary support, which was "difficult to sustain within current funding models".

Head of the Health Economics Group at Monash University's School of Public Health and Preventative Medicine, Professor Cathy Mihalopoulos, told SBS News GPs respond to a range of mental health conditions.

She said they most commonly see a "breadth of severity" in "high prevalence" conditions such as anxiety and depression.

"For a lot of GPs, the commitment is to do the best they can for the person sitting in front of them ... they absolutely want to do the best they can, but the problems they're confronted with often aren't something you can easily solve in five minutes," she said.

The health economist said part of the pressure on GPs is a lack of services for the "missing middle" — patients whose needs sit between what a GP and a specialised service provides.

"These are people who are not mild, and they're not very severe .... they're in that missing middle," she said.

"Their care often falls to GPs, but their care is quite complex in terms of the things they may have to deal with."

She said GPs play a crucial role in helping those seeking support for their mental health to navigate a "fragmented" health system.

The report also found GPs were helping alleviate pressure on hospital services and bridge gaps in the healthcare system.

In 2026, almost 90 per cent of GPs managed conditions usually treated by non-GP specialists, and 76 per cent managed conditions typically treated in emergency departments or urgent care settings.

Bulk billing increases

The proportion of patients bulk billed for all GP visits rose to 63 per cent in 2026, up from 56 per cent in each of the previous two years, which the report attributed to increased Medicare incentives.

RACGP president Dr Michael Wright said increased government investment in Medicare to $489 per person in 2026 was an important recognition of general practice's role in Australian healthcare, but that more investment was needed to cover longer consultations.

"The challenge is that the Medicare system has not kept pace with the realities of modern general practice, and funding does not adequately support the time required to provide the care patients need."

Bulk billing incentives have reduced out-of-pocket costs, but some Australians are still delaying their healthcare. Source: AAP / Darren England

The rate of Australians delaying seeking healthcare due to cost fell from 8.8 per cent in 2025 to 7.7 per cent in 2026. Young adults aged 25 to 34 remain the most likely to delay care because of cost.

Mihalopoulos said it remains a "real problem".

"We should not be delaying seeking care for our health, because everything depends on our good health," she said.

She said while bulk billing incentives have contributed to increased presentations, Australia is not "100 per cent there yet".

"Getting people into care earlier and addressing their needs is crucial."

Intersectional outcomes

For the first time, women GPs reported less satisfaction with their jobs than their male counterparts, with the proportion of female GPs recommending the profession to younger colleagues dropping from 53 per cent in 2025 to 48 per cent in 2026.

In 2026, female GPs saw a higher proportion of patients presenting with complex psycho-social issues, mental health concerns and women's health matters, and spent more time with patients on average than their male counterparts.

Racism was also identified as part of some GPs' experience, with more than 30 per cent agreeing that they had witnessed racism towards patients within the broader healthcare system, and 19 per cent reporting personally experiencing racism in the past year.

While 6 per cent of GPs said they had personally experienced racism from a colleague within their practice, 65 per cent said they were confident in addressing or challenging racism from patients or colleagues within their practice and the broader healthcare system.

title: Wells says Bluey reflects Australian values while Joyce criticises intolerance of satire
text:
IN BRIEF One Nation is under fire for its use of Bluey in a 2024 episode of the party's Please Explain series.

In the episode, it's implied that Bluey mows down Daniel Andrews and Anthony Albanese with a car.

Communications Minister Anika Wells says the ABC is "well within its rights" to be concerned about a One Nation video in which its beloved character Bluey is run over by a car.

The Australian cartoon dog appeared in a 2024 episode of One Nation's Please Explain series, now the subject of legal action by the ABC.

In the episode, a car driven by former Victorian premier Daniel Andrews hits Bluey, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in the passenger seat.

The episode implies the battered Bluey mows down the premier and prime minister later in the episode, titled The State of Melbourne.

"Bluey is one of Australia's biggest, most large, most well-known exports. I think the ABC's well within its rights to be concerned here," Wells told ABC RN on Wednesday morning.

Wells acknowledged the video series is satirical, but said there is a line between satirising politics and making a politician's life "unbearable".

"It's certainly not something that I would produce or that I would ever ask my team to produce," she said.

'We will be taking further action'

ABC managing director Hugh Marks said it was a "shocking use of Australia's most loved character" in a Senate estimates hearing on Tuesday.

"Probably the globally most loved character in a video that is both shocking and disrespectful to the children of Australia," he said.

"I can't substantiate it either legally, or on the basis of its usage."

Labor senator Varun Ghosh described Bluey's use as "heinous", particularly in light of the alleged attack on independent MP Helen Haines on 19 October, where she was hit by a car and lost both legs.

To Marks' knowledge, One Nation had not licensed Bluey's likeness from BBC Studios, which distributes the TV show, but could still be entitled to show the character under fair use provisions if Please Explain is considered satire or parody.

But the ABC boss said he did not think that defence would suffice.

"It's not a parody of any Bluey work, it's not a minor use of the (intellectual property). In my view, it is an infringement of the intellectual property," he said.

"I think it's a blatant use.

"We will be taking further action. I can assure you."

The broadcaster will write One Nation a cease and desist letter demanding the video be taken down, with Marks flagging it may seek damages.

The party used Bluey in another Please Explain episode about Queensland, where the dog did not drive into any politicians.

Wells declined to comment on any legal proceedings when asked, but she added: "Bluey has a lot more production value than One Nation's cartoons. We can all learn a lot from Bluey."

Joyce accuses critics of 'sanitising beyond satire'

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce has said the Please Explain cartoons were satire and were not meant to be taken seriously.

"You get to a point where you are sanitising beyond satire and you are starting to put restrictions on us," he told ABC TV on Tuesday.

"You've got to have some form of tolerance."

Joyce has previously apologised for another One Nation cartoon calling Liberal frontbencher and former Special Air Services soldier Andrew Hastie a "traitor".

title: A missing link to Australia's newest airport comes with a $55 sting
text:
in brief Western Sydney International Airport travellers face public transport stopgaps.

The promised metro line to the airport may not be operational until mid 2028.

Western Sydney International Airport (WSI)'s opening marks Australia's first major new aviation gateway in over half a century, yet it will be a long time before visitors will be able to take a train to or from the terminal.

From its outset, state and transit authorities had promised that WSI would come complete with a high-speed, driverless metro line to connect passengers to the wider Sydney rail network.

However, disputes with contractors, corruption allegations, and deadline blowouts have left staff and travellers forced to use stop-gap methods to reach the airport, with alternative arrangements unlikely to materialise for well over a year.

In June, the NSW government was forced to concede that the delays to the metro line opening could continue until mid-2028 — some 18 months after the grand opening of WSI.

While construction delays continue, travellers and staff face limited public transport options, with private firms' alternatives costing up to $55 per person.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Temporary transport measures

While the NSW government and Sydney Metro maintained that the metro line connecting Badgerys Creek to Bradfield and St Marys would open on schedule, planning for an emergency alternative began in early 2025, internal policy documents later revealed.

After spending $11 billion on an incomplete metro line, the NSW government announced earlier this month that the WSI Link free shuttle service would ferry passengers the 20km shortfall between the terminal and St Marys railway station on the T1 Western Line.

Five suburban bus routes have also been re-routed to the airport precinct to deliver travellers to Mount Druitt, Penrith, Liverpool, Campbelltown and Leppington at standard rates.

The WSI Link shuttle bus runs every 30 minutes from 4.30am to midnight, Sunday to Thursday, and until 1am on Friday and Saturday.

Other travel options to the city

Private operator Super Shuttle WSI offers an express coach service to Parramatta, the Sydney CBD and Sydney Airport (Kingsford Smith). A single adult ticket to Parramatta costs $25 and a return $45, the single/return adult fares to the Sydney CBD are $55/$80 and for Sydney Airport they are $65/$90.

One of the primary advantages of WSI over Sydney's original Kingsford Smith Airport is its lack of curfew, allowing passengers to arrive and depart 24 hours a day. However, current public transport services keep to standard operational hours, potentially leaving some passengers and staff with limited early-morning options.

Transport for NSW defended the interim transit arrangements, stating operating hours reflect current scheduling.

"There are currently no passenger flights operating or at this moment planned between 1 and 4.30am through Western Sydney International Airport," a Transport for NSW spokesperson told SBS News. "Transport for NSW continues to monitor service demand as the airport grows."

The department said travellers arriving during the overnight window have access to private shuttles, rideshares, and vehicle parking.

While current schedules favour daytime hours, international and budget carriers are scheduled to scale up through early 2027.

Western Sydney International's limitations 'understood'

Adam Leto, CEO of the Western Sydney Leadership Dialogue, told SBS News that the airport ought to be seen in its broader context and that initial concerns over transport pale in comparison to the benefit it brings.

"Rome wasn't built in a day," Leto said. "We've understood what the airport was going to look like when it opened, and it's not going to be the full picture. I think most people in western Sydney understood that and accepted that."

Leto noted that the surrounding road network, including the newly opened M12 motorway, was always expected to carry the bulk of early passenger movements but that it will need to adapt as passenger numbers swell.

The six-station Western Sydney International Airport metro line is expected as early as late 2027, but could be pushed back to mid 2028.

"This is about what's happening over the next 20 — 30 years, not what happens over the next 20 — 30 days," he said. "I think there's going to be more infrastructure that will be required to support the growth of the airport."

Round-the-clock transport will take time to mature, Leto said.

"We've never had a 24-hour airport, so it's a new thing for Sydney to grapple with and understand and learn how to leverage."

However, local government leaders have warned that interim solutions must not displace long-term public transport commitments.

Penrith mayor Todd Carney said the completed metro line to St Marys would eventually be a "gamechanger", but called on the state government to fund the full north-south rail link. The route linking St Marys to Tallawong and Bradfield to Macarthur remains in the early planning stages.

"Ours is one of the fastest-growing regions in the country and with that growth comes enormous opportunity," Carney said. "However, communities can only benefit from opportunity if they can access it.''

The rail delivery timeline blew out after lead contractor Webuild lodged claims for around $2.2 billion in contract variations, slowing station works.

The dispute was compounded when an independent probity investigation uncovered invoicing and payroll irregularities among subcontractors, triggering referrals to the police, the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption, and the National Anti-Corruption Commission.

Commercial passenger services on the airport metro line are now not expected to run until late 2027 at the earliest, with Premier Chris Minns revealing in June that services may not open until mid 2028.

title: The 'growing' health threat now responsible for one in 10 Australian deaths
text:
In Brief Dementia caused more than 10 per cent of deaths in Australia last year.

The figure increased by almost 40 per cent in the past decade, while deaths due to heart diseases decreased.

Dementia now accounts for more than one in 10 Australian deaths for the first time as advocates warn of a continued surge in the condition as the population ages.

More than 19,000 people (10.1 per cent) died from dementia, including Alzheimer's disease, in 2025, according to analysis released on Tuesday as part of the Australian Bureau of Statistics' (ABS) Causes of Death report.

Dementia has been the leading cause of death for women in Australia since 2016, and in 2024 it overtook cancer and heart disease to become Australia's leading killer nationally.

This is the first time dementia deaths have exceeded 10 per cent, more than double the rates reported in 2006, when dementia was the fourth-leading cause of death nationally.

Dementia Australia's chief executive officer, professor Tanya Buchanan, said the new data reinforced the urgent need to raise awareness of the condition as a leading public health issue affecting Australians.

"The data underlines the critical need for more recognition and funding to support people living with dementia, their families and carers," Buchanan said in a statement.

"Despite the growing impact of dementia, investment in specific services, supports and prevention has not kept the same pace, and the stigma that surrounds dementia continues. This needs to change."

Buchanan said that with nearly 500,000 Australians living with dementia, without "significant intervention", the figure was expected to increase to more than one million by 2065.

A gendered killer

In 2025, women accounted for more than 60 per cent of all deaths attributed to dementia in Australia.

The report found that there were almost twice as many deaths from dementia as from ischaemic heart diseases, which is the second leading cause of death for women.

The ABS said that in 2025, there were just 2,791 deaths separating the top two leading causes of death, with that gap continuing to widen as dementia deaths increase over time, and deaths from ischaemic heart disease continued to decline.

Between 2016 and 2025, the number of deaths due to dementia increased by 37 per cent, while deaths due to ischaemic heart diseases and cerebrovascular diseases decreased by 16.2 per cent and 12.1 per cent, respectively.

The mortality rate for ischaemic heart diseases was the lowest on record since its peak in 1968.

After ischaemic heart diseases and cerebrovascular diseases, lung cancer and chronic lower respiratory diseases rounded the top five leading causes of death, which in 2025 represented more than 30 per cent of all registered deaths.

The Marrickville Golf Club was in a stink. A new clientele of families and young revellers drawn to its coveted spot on the banks of the Cooks River had helped its bottom line, but the club’s ancient septic system was struggling to cope. The Marrickville Golf Club, in Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s seat of Grayndler, is in the centre of a political firestorm. Audrey Richardson Repeated failures had led to sewage flowing onto the course, and potentially into the river itself. As the NSW Department of Crown Lands diplomatically described it last year, the failure of the septic system had led to “discharged wastewater” which was “impacting golfers, recreational walkers and presenting an environmental risk” to the river.

Advertisement

For a club mindful of its place in the left-wing, environmentally conscious inner west – not to mention the olfactory senses of its golfers – it was a major issue. Though management had for years sought funding for various upgrades, it was desperate for a quick fix. So, the club reached out to Anthony Albanese’s office for help. Sources close to the golf club familiar with the negotiations, speaking on the condition of anonymity so they could speak freely, told this masthead the club first went to the prime minister’s office seeking help after a redistribution moved it from the electorate of Barton to his seat of Grayndler before the last election. In accounts which lend credibility to Albanese’s initial, incorrect claim about the $6 million grant, those sources said the early conversations were about fixing the club’s long-standing sewage problem. Those conversations were not with Albanese himself, but members of his local electorate office. About the same time, club sources said, it asked others – including state MP Jo Haylen, the member for Summer Hill – for help too.

Advertisement

Haylen approached Steve Kamper, the NSW minister for Crown lands, who approved a $269,500 grant to connect the clubhouse to the mains sewer in September 2025. Though it was a discretionary grant, the money, from a Crown Lands fund, was assessed by the department before it was approved and found to have met the assessment criteria for funding. Since the scandal broke, colleagues have jokingly referred to the minister as “Kenny Kamper”, a reference to the 2006 Shane Jacobson mockumentary Kenny about a plumber. While it remains unclear how exactly the request for a new sewerage system turned into a $6 million federal grant, Inner West Mayor Darcy Byrne said the club had been seeking funds for a renovation for several years.

Advertisement

“The club has been advocating for funding to renovate the clubhouse, which is essentially a fibro shack, for close to a decade,” Byrne, a long-time political ally of Albanese, told a Senate inquiry. “When people say Royal Marrickville, that’s a joke because it’s such a working-class institution.” The club has found itself at the centre of a political firestorm since controversy over the grant first emerged last month. Its general manager, Mathew Ward, declined to comment when approached. However, this masthead is aware the club and its staff have been subject to trolling online and in phone calls as a result of the grant furore. Albanese has faced fierce criticism after admitting the $6 million grant was not designed to fund sewerage works. That admission came after bureaucrats contradicted his previous claims, revealing the money was earmarked for a series of other upgrades including a renovation of its clubhouse and a new pro shop.

Advertisement

Coalition senator James Paterson on Thursday said the prime minister’s repeated claims about the sewage issue exposed a lack of integrity in the government. “Whenever you make a false statement, as soon as you become aware of it, you are obliged to go at the earliest opportunity to correct the record. He did not do so,” Paterson said. “In years gone by, this would have cost a minister their job. Under Albanese’s government, there are no standards at all.” Women’s Golf Committee president Julie Granger said some members didn’t want such a large grant. Audrey Richardson The $6 million grant included $4.55 million for upgrades to the clubhouse, $1 million for stormwater harvesting and another $500,000 for new “botanic plantings” and landscaping. That work has yet to begin. Though the prime minister has sought to distance himself, the boost has been referred to by the club as the “Albanese upgrades” or “Albanese building works” in newsletters to members.

Advertisement

Nestled on the banks of the Cooks River, the club is an inner west institution that holds specific importance for the local Labor Party fraternity. In 2020, senior Labor figures, including Albanese, defeated a Greens-led proposal to reduce the course to nine holes. The campaign was seen as an important victory in an area that has threatened to drift towards the Greens in recent elections. Unlike most golf clubs, Marrickville has long been a refuge for a largely working-class clientele. However, the club has increasingly gentrified along with the suburb of Marrickville. Additions, such as a new restaurant, have made it popular with a wider crowd. Gerri Shaw, a member of 16 years, says the money has destroyed Marrickville Golf Club. Audrey Richardson The club held an information session with members last Tuesday, and has laid out plans for a refurbishment of the existing clubhouse interior, a new and upgraded bar area, an expanded deck and covered outdoor areas, new public toilets and additional “family friendly” outdoor space. Those changes have sometimes irritated long-standing members. Some were angry when a putting green on the lawn of the clubhouse was turned into an outdoor eating area favoured by families, and its new popularity is not universally appreciated.

“Getting that money has destroyed the club,” Gerri Shaw, a member of 16 years, said on Thursday. “I think the clubhouse needs some work, but now that it’s become what they call a community club on a weekend, this is packed out with young families and kids running riot … I don’t come near this place on a weekend any more.” President of the club’s women’s golf committee Julie Granger said some members would have preferred to avoid such a large grant, and complained the renovation plans went beyond what members wanted. “Some people have said that it was probably the death knell of the club. It needn’t have been, had it been used with the members in mind instead of the bistro,” Granger said. title: They called him ‘Temu Postecoglou’. Now this Aussie coach has Beckham and Co in his corner
text:
Advertisement

SportSoccerEngland They called him ‘Temu Postecoglou’. Now this Aussie coach has Beckham and Co in his corner Vince Rugari October 29, 2026 — 3:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Peter Cklamovski has spent more time than anyone else riding shotgun with Ange Postecoglou - so for him, a rocky start to a new job is not just familiar terrain, but preferred. This time around, the rocks were extra jagged. Loading Being a self-proclaimed Postecoglou “disciple” was an advantage not so long ago. Now, post-Tottenham, and post-Nottingham, Postecoglou’s reputation in England has taken a battering, as unfair as that may be, to the point where even those who have worked with him are tainted by association. So when Cklamovski lost his first three matches in charge of English fourth-division club Salford City this season, some online critics swiftly settled on a nickname for him: ‘Temu Postecoglou’. Or ‘Temu Ange’, or any such derivative. The inference is clear, and it stings: he is a lesser version of a coach they don’t rate.

Advertisement

Cklamovski can only chuckle. “That’s modern-day football, modern-day society,” he tells this masthead. Peter Cklamovski and his long-time mentor, Ange Postecoglou, after a match between Shimizu S-Pulse and Yokohama F. Marinos. Getty “I’m proud of my connection with Ange, and I want to be a proud extension of his legacy. That’s how much I love the guy. Within that, there’s no secrets. They know, they’ve learned that I’m an Ange disciple, let’s say - so I guess there is a bit of a stigma to that, potentially. “But that’s all noise. If I do my job, and do it well, and do it the way I know I can, then that will be the way we can build something that we dream about. Stay humble, take the bullets when needed, no problem - but don’t let it knock you down.”

Advertisement

Such is the fickle nature of the game that those same supporters who wanted him gone a couple of months ago are probably now singing his name. Salford City are cruising on top of the table amid a club-record seven-game winning streak, and Cklamovski has just been named League Two’s manager of the month. It’s still early days - there are still 33 more games to be played this season - but they are hot favourites to be promoted, and some of the sport’s biggest names are swooning about the aggressive and relentless attacking football Cklamovski has them playing. Jorge Grant celebrates a goal for Salford City against Walsall. Getty Images Indeed, this is no ordinary club. Of all the teams in England’s Football League - the umbrella organisation for the three tiers below the Premier League - Salford City is arguably the best-placed to trace a similar arc as Wrexham and rise up the pyramid, powered by celebrity investment.

Advertisement

Actually, they kind of invented the concept of ‘doing a Wrexham’. In 2014, five members of Manchester United’s fabled Class of ’92 - Gary Neville, Phil Neville, Paul Scholes, Ryan Giggs and Nicky Butt - purchased the club, which is only a short drive from Old Trafford, and only a kilometre from where they used to train together. David Beckham later joined the ownership group, and their early efforts to lift the then-little-known club from the obscurity of England’s eighth division were captured in a fly-on-the-wall documentary by the BBC. Salford City co-owners Gary Neville and David Beckham. Salford City FC But after four promotions in five years, their progress stalled, and the ‘Ammies’ - a nickname taken from the club’s old name, Salford Amateurs - have been stuck in League Two for the past seven seasons. Most of the former players sold up as part of a recent ownership restructure which brought in fresh international capital - but Beckham and Gary Neville retained their shares, and their new ambition is to eventually bring Salford City into the Premier League.

Advertisement

The club has also gone back to its roots, reverting to its traditional orange colours this season and ditching the United-inspired red shirts introduced by the ex-players - a decision Gary Neville has since admitted was “quite selfish” and an error he was happy to rectify. League Two was not exactly top of Cklamovski’s list for his next job, but when the opportunity to join Salford City bobbed up while on holiday in England with his family, and he came to understand the scale of their project, he couldn’t say no. The initial approach was made by Gavin Fleig, a former City Football Group executive who now runs Salford City, and who knew Cklamovski from his time working under Postecoglou at Yokohama F. Marinos, a CFG partner club. Cklamovski, 48, was Postecoglou’s assistant in a variety of roles for more than a decade, but branched out on his own after lifting the Japanese title with Yokohama in 2019, and most recently was coach of the Malaysian national team.

Advertisement

Scholes no longer holds his 10 per cent stake, but remains at the club as chief football advisor. He was not alone in needing to look up Cklamovski’s name, but was blown away by his interview. “Peter was very impressive, right from the word go,” he said in a club feature on YouTube. Salford City chief football advisor Paul Scholes and coach Peter Cklamovski. Salford City FC Now Scholes watches the first team train most days, and acts as a valuable sounding board for Cklamovski. “He’s around for anything I need, really ... a really good eye for League Two because he’s been watching it for a decade or so, intimately,” Cklamovski says. “For me, that’s a depth of knowledge that I can always lean on.”

Advertisement

Other ex-United legends, including Roy Keane, routinely turn up for matches at their 2,246-seat home ground, Moor Lane, and more will jump on the bandwagon if their current form continues. After their most recent performance, a 4-2 victory over previously unbeaten Walsall, Gary Neville said he’d never seen Salford City play better football. With all the star power surrounding him, Cklamovski has to keep a deliberately narrow focus. ‘That’s a depth of knowledge that I can always lean on.’ Peter Cklamovski on working with Paul Scholes “There might be a bit of glitz and glamour in and around the club, but if I take my eye off what’s the most important thing, which is to get the football right, then I’m not doing my job,” he says. “The club has lofty ambitions, that’s for sure, and it’s being met with a solid plan. My job here is to put the foundation of the football in place ... build that identity of football for Salford City and, along with that, push hard and achieve success and get the club stepping up the English pyramid.“

Advertisement

For Cklamovski, that means doing what he has always done: trusting the process, even when it may feel like the walls are closing in on him. After those three first-up defeats, a fourth beckoned, and questions about his future would have surely followed. Salford were at home to Newport County and absolutely dominating - they finished with 31 shots to 4 - but it was one of those games when the ball just wouldn’t go in. Naturally, they went down 1-0 in the 71st minute, conceding a freakish long-range goal in which their goalkeeper was lobbed from 60 metres out. Peter Cklamovski. Getty Images “I’m thinking, ‘Oh no, not this again,’” Cklamovski says. “But there was a part inside me that was loving it. Seen it before, lived it before. I just knew that this is going to add to the story.”

Advertisement

Salford scored twice in the final 10 minutes, including a 90th-minute winner to prevail 2-1. Cklamovski looks back on it as the “circuit breaker” moment when his players were rewarded for refusing to abandon their principles - a familiar juncture for teams schooled in the ways of Angeball. Related Article Opinion

England The Ballon d’Or is everything football shouldn’t be. Thank goodness for Harry Kane Vince Rugari Reporter “I knew we were on track,” Cklamovski says. “I knew the boys were believing in the football, that the evidence was there on the pitch. They felt it. They saw it. They trained it.” The wins have flowed freely ever since, but there will be potholes in the road ahead. Cklamovski is encountering all the unique challenges of England’s lower professional leagues: the physicality is high, the stadiums almost uncomfortably intimate, the supporters fiercely passionate, while games can descend into disorder without warning. “There can be a lot of chaos in a game,” he says.

Advertisement

“It might be a referee call, it might be a tough away game, and the crowd get on top of you ... but chaos can get created very easily in this league. If we can control that chaos and play our football, then that control becomes a bit of a weapon.” It’s been a major change of pace for Cklamovski, who was accustomed to coaching in front of huge crowds in high-profile gigs in charge of FC Tokyo and Malaysia. Now he’s criss-crossing the heartlands of English football, working out of tiny grounds and falling for the peculiar romance of the lower leagues - all while trying to build something that he believes will one day find its way to a much bigger stage. “It’s humble beginnings right now,” he says. “But I’m sure in 12 months, 18 months, two years’ time - whether I’m here or not - the club will be a bigger brand, a bigger football club. You’ll see this place in a really innovative sort of spot where it’s building, and building something special. To be a small part of that, mate, it’s exciting.”

After a post-pandemic dip, Perth Festival is back doing what patrons want it to do: deliver the best in international arts and culture. Even though it’s been six years since COVID shut the world down, it has taken that long for the international arts touring scene to get back on track and for Perth Festival to be once again on global touring itineraries. Perth Festival artistic director Anna Reece. Frances Andrijich During that period, successive Perth Festival artistic directors have been forced to call upon local companies and artists to make up the numbers. While it has provided opportunities for local practitioners, it also led to a rumbling among patrons, who complained the city’s premier arts festival was not doing its job.

Advertisement

That longing for large-scale world-class works will be satisfied in 2027, which will be a series of European blockbuster shows that hark back to Perth Festival’s glory days, such as Peter Brook’s nine-hour Mahabharata in the Boya Quarry (back in 1988), and Robert Lepage’s Seven Streams of the River Ota in 1998, transformative experiences that still burn bright in the memory. “Perth deserves to experience some of the best, most exciting artists and ideas from around the world.” Perth Festival artistic director Anna Reece From Latvia comes trailblazing Polish director Łukasz Twarkowski’s ROTHKO, a four-hour time-shifting collision of cinema and theatre inspired by a famous art forgery; from Denmark comes Operation: Orfeo, a “hypnotic reimagining of the Greek myth of Orpheus and Eurydice told through extraordinary voices, light, architecture and illusion”; and from Greece comes Taverna Miresia – Mario, Bella, Anastasia, Mario Banushi’s wordless and visually stunning evocation of his Albanian childhood that recently won the Golden Lion at the Venice Biennale. Perth Festival artistic director Anna Reece was unapologetic about the pivot to the international for next year’s late-summer arts jamboree. “We are an international arts festival, and we should be proud of that. It is also our point of difference within the local scene,” Reece said ahead of Thursday’s program unveiling at the East Perth Power Station, which the Festival has brought back from the dead in the past two years.

Advertisement

“Over the past couple of years we’ve worked really hard to create a distinct identity for Perth Festival. “We have created new spaces for Perth people to gather and experience art, such as the Power Station and The Embassy Ballroom in the Perth Town Hall. Perth Festival will again take over the East Perth Power Station this year. Jessica Wyld Photography “These are now familiar gathering points that are critical for the Festival. “With those foundations in place we are ready to expand our international ambition again. Perth deserves to experience some of the best, most exciting artists and ideas from around the world.”

Advertisement

Reece said Perth Festival’s re-embracing of its international ambition, upon which it built its reputation, did not mean local practitioners would be overlooked. Editor's pick Marine life Where have the calves gone? The troubling shift in Australia’s whale highways “A great international arts festival should expand our sense of what’s possible at the same time as strengthening our commitment to WA artists. The two make each other stronger,” she said. “There were a number of local commissions last year and there will be another wave 2028. “It has to do with the cycles and the time it takes to complete work.

Advertisement

“International work challenges us and it challenges our local artists. It broadens our perspective and connects our city to conversations happening far beyond our borders.” Reece is reluctant to dive back into COVID – “it’s boring,” she laughs – but emphasised the damage the pandemic did to arts festivals around the world. Łukasz Twarkowski’s ROTHKO. “The knock-on effect of COVID has been enormous,” she said. “Everything stopped. It meant you couldn’t tap into the tours of European companies.

Advertisement

“If you wanted the work, they had to come back together and rehearse it. The global pipeline dried up. “Perth Festival over the years has hosted some of the great masters, such as Robert Lepage. This year we are introducing local audiences to the next generation of superstars, such as Łukasz Twarkowski and Mario Banushi. It’s incredibly exciting.” Perth Festival runs from February 5 to 28. Tickets for all shows are on sale from November 2. Lotterywest Films begins on November 23 with Jesse Eisenberg’s The Debut.

Victor Radley is eager to strike a new deal with the Roosters, but has conceded that he will entertain offers from NRL rivals – and even the Super League – for the first time in his career so he can look after his young family. Amid the exodus of stars including Mark Nawaqanitawase, Daly Cherry-Evans, Angus Crichton and Spencer Leniu that followed the Roosters’ premiership win, and this week’s headlines surrounding Sam Walker’s messy contract situation, it is easy to forget Radley will hit the open market for the first time on Sunday. Victor Radley trains with the England team in Wollongong on Thursday. Peter Keleman/SWpix.com The 28-year-old enforcer has spent a decade in the NRL, winning three premierships with the Roosters, and has never felt the need to explore what might be out there beyond the eastern suburbs – until now. Radley is in no rush to sort his future as he finalises his departure from long-time agent Sam Ayoub before joining a new management team.

Advertisement

The hard-hitting forward’s preference is to finish a one-club player, but said it was important his next contract was one that looked after his fiancée Taylah and two young boys, Vinnie and Cruze. If Radley, a local junior, cannot agree to a new deal with the Roosters, he is open to linking with an NRL rival – including the PNG Chiefs – or even a move to England, the country he will represent in the World Cup on Friday night against Papua New Guinea in Wollongong. Victor Radley with fiancée Taylah and sons Vinnie and Cruze after the Roosters’ grand final win earlier this month. Instagram “The Roosters are everything I’ve ever known,” Radley told this masthead. “I love the club so much. They’ve done right by me for years. “It hurts me inside just thinking about playing elsewhere, but I need to look at all my options now. The days are gone where I’m living in a two-bedroom unit, having a good time. I have two kids, a fiancée, and a house that needs paying off.

Advertisement

“Like everyone in Australia, you have your struggles with interest rates. People will laugh at that and say, ‘He’s been on good money’. But I’ve got a decent mortgage. “I also copped some financial pain at the end of last year [The Roosters hit Radley with a $150,000 penalty for bringing the club into disrepute during a Sunshine Coast golf trip]. “It hurts me inside just thinking about playing elsewhere, but I need to look at all my options now. I have two kids, a fiancée, and a house that needs paying off.” Victor Radley “I’m open to everything. I love new experiences, that might even include living in England and playing in the Super League. It’s something I’d be interested in.” Radley’s immediate focus, though, is finalising his management situation. “I’m joining a new company run by my fiancée’s uncle [Paul Williams] who has brought on board my good friend Max Muddle. I’m excited about that. We’ll sit down on Monday and work out what we want to do moving forward.”

Advertisement

Radley has a long history of head knocks but insisted there was no cause for prospective new clubs to be alarmed. He only missed one through game concussion in 2026 after a desperate tackle in the 80th minutes against the Wests Tigers saw him come off second best. Related Video Video icon 2:13 Kangaroos stars dragged into Walker saga “I understood what happened to me at the start of last year – I was in that state of chronic fatigue, which is why I kept getting those concussions,” Radley said. “I worked hard with the staff to make sure I never get into that state of fatigue again, and the proof has been in the pudding with just the one [head knock this year].” Radley backed Dolphins star and England teammate Herbie Farnworth to join the Roosters, a move which has been the subject of heavy speculation for most of this year.

“He’s a quality player,” Radley said. “I’ve said it since 2022 [when I first met him with England]. When you see how hard he works at training, he’ll be a quality player for any team – and hopefully it’s us.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday. London/Nassau: King Charles danced in the street with a troupe of dancers in the Bahamas on Wednesday, the second day of a royal visit to the Caribbean that has been somewhat overshadowed by increasingly vocal demands for Britain to pay reparations for its role in the slave trade. Wielding a pair of cowbells in the colours of the flag of the Bahamas, Charles took part in a traditional Junkanoo – a carnival event celebrating the island’s culture. King Charles shakes traditional cowbells at the head of the Bahamian Junkanoo. AP Dressed in a suit and sunglasses, the King cut a dapper figure at the front of the parade among the feathered headdresses and colourful costumes of the dancers, and was met with cheers by the crowd. He began the day by paying respects to fallen members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force, laying a wreath at the Flamingo Monument, and later visited the Bahamas Boxing Academy, where he was presented with a T-shirt bearing an image of himself wearing a champion’s belt.

Advertisement

Loading Arriving in the Bahamas on Tuesday for his first visit as King, Charles acknowledged the injustices of slavery, saying Commonwealth leaders would discuss the issue at their summit next week. Charles meets a young boxer at the Bahamas Boxing Academy in Nassau. Getty Images Speaking in the Bahamian capital Nassau at the start of a three-day trip, the King said it was “only right” to acknowledge “the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond”. Charles added that some of what was “best” in Bahamian culture today – “the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright” – was “born out of darkness”.

Advertisement

His remarks come before the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda next week, where regional leaders are expected to press demands for reparations for slavery and colonialism. Jamaica recently took its claim for reparations to Charles, and the case has since been referred to the UK’s highest court of appeal for the Caribbean island. The British government, however, has consistently rejected demands for either an apology or reparations. ‘Pay us what you owe us’ In Nassau, members of the islands’ Rastafarian community and others staged a demonstration near Clifford Park, where the King met local students, demanding reparations. “Pay us what you owe us!” one woman cried out. “I stand in memory of the horrors and the atrocities committed against black people.” Members of the Ethiopian African Black International Congress stage a demonstration in downtown Nassau. AP

Advertisement

Charles will visit Guyana next before travelling to Antigua and Barbuda where he will be joined by his wife, Queen Camilla, for the biennial summit of the Commonwealth which comprises 56 nations, mostly former British colonies. Related Article Analysis

International affairs King underlines peacemaker role as row hangs over Commonwealth summit The issue of reparations has gathered momentum across the Caribbean recently. Last month, CARICOM, the regional bloc, said it wanted the matter on the agenda at the summit. “The Caribbean has consistently asserted that reparations is fundamentally about justice,” CARICOM Secretary-General Carla Barnett said last month. Buckingham Palace had indicated that the King would address the issue during the tour, but not offer a formal apology, in line with British government policy, which also rules out financial reparations.

Advertisement

Charles inspects an honour guard of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force. AP A palace spokesperson said the visit would focus mainly on “modern partnerships and opportunities for the future” in the region, but added that for Charles it was also part of “a lifelong” effort to engage with and educate about “the most shameful aspects of our past”. Campaigners and some Caribbean leaders have called on Britain to go further, including through an apology, reparations in the form of financial compensation and the return of cultural artefacts. From the 15th to the 19th century, at least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into slavery by European traders, with Britain transporting an estimated 3.2 million people across the Atlantic, making it one of the biggest slave-trading nations. title: Consumers are mincemeat, but the RBA keeps raising the heat
text:

BusinessThe economyInflation Consumers are mincemeat, but the RBA keeps raising the heat Colin Kruger October 29, 2026 — 3:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
